docs.title: Rules that apply to every idea
docs.text:
These come from the detailed plans and are not repeated in each entry.

  • Every fact shown carries its source document, page and quote. No source, no claim.
  • Show records, not verdicts. Patterns are "worth checking", never proof of wrongdoing.
  • Officials appear by post. Elected representatives appear in their public role only.
  • Residents' photos have faces and number plates blurred before storage.
  • Nothing about a named party is published without a person reviewing it first.
  • Do not defeat access controls such as captchas. Ask for data, or collect it by hand at a polite rate.

docs.title: Money: where it is allocated and whether it is spent
docs.text: Ideas 6 to 13. Idea 1, Paisa Trail, is in ../mumbai-civic-graph/01-paisa-trail.md.

docs.title: 6. Unspent Money Watch
docs.text:
Problem. Each February the budget announces large allocations. Press reports on civic data showed more than half of the 2025-26 capital budget unspent late in that year. The gap between what is announced and what is spent is rarely visible by department or by ward.

What residents get. For each department and budget head: the budget estimate, the revised estimate and the actual spend, for the last five years, on one line. A plain sentence under it: "Storm water drains were given ₹X; ₹Y was spent; this has happened three years running."

Data. Budget books only. Each year's book prints the previous years' revised estimates and actuals beside the new estimates.

How. The intake desk parses budget tables into Allocation nodes with amount_be, amount_re, amount_actual per FiscalYear. The rest is arithmetic in code. An agent writes the plain-language line and flags heads that are under-spent every year.

First version. Days. One department, five years.

Watch out. Under-spending has innocent causes (court stays, land not handed over, monsoon). Show the number and ask the question; do not explain it without a source. Totals must reconcile with the printed department total before anything is shown.

docs.title: 7. Ward Budget in Plain Words
docs.text:
Problem. The budget is hundreds of pages of codes. A resident cannot tell what it means for their ward.

What residents get. A two-page summary per ward in Marathi, Hindi and English: the works named for the ward this year, what they cost, last year's list and what happened to it. Readable aloud at a residents' meeting. Shareable as an image.

Data. Budget books, ward-wise works lists where the budget prints them, and the tender graph for status.

How. Works are linked to wards in the graph. The drafter agent writes the summary from graph facts only; the rubric requires a source for every figure and bans jargon. A person fluent in Marathi reviews before release.

First version. Days, for one ward.

Watch out. Many budget lines are citywide and cannot honestly be split by ward. Say so and list them separately.

docs.title: 8. Corporator Fund Tracker
docs.text:
Problem. Each corporator has discretionary funds for small local works. Residents seldom know what their corporator chose to spend it on, or whether the benches, lights and paver blocks appeared.

What residents get. Per electoral ward: the fund available, each work sanctioned from it, its cost, and its location on a map. A button to confirm with a photo whether the work exists.

Data. Ward office sanction records. Probably not published in usable form; needs RTI to each ward office or cooperation from corporators who are willing to publish their own.

How. (Work)-[:FUNDED_BY]->(Allocation {kind: 'corporator_fund'}) and (Person)-[:SANCTIONED]->(Work). The RTI drafter produces one application per ward office. Replies come back as scans; the intake desk reads them.

First version. Weeks, because of the RTI wait. Start with two or three corporators who volunteer their lists.

Watch out. Starting with volunteers rewards the transparent ones; frame it that way.

docs.title: 9. MP and MLA Fund Tracker
docs.text:
Problem. Members of Parliament and of the state assembly also have local area development funds spent in Mumbai. Works funded this way are executed through district and civic agencies and are hard to tell apart from civic works.

What residents get. For each Mumbai constituency: works recommended, sanctioned and completed, with cost and location, alongside the civic works on the same map.

Data. The national MPLADS scheme publishes work-level data. State MLA fund data is less consistent. Confirm what is available for Mumbai's constituencies.

How. A second Agency and funding source in the same ontology. Constituency boundaries are overlaid on wards.

First version. Days for MPs if the published data is usable.

Watch out. Keep the three kinds of fund (civic, MLA, MP) visibly separate so nobody is credited or blamed for another's work.

docs.title: 10. Rate Card
docs.text:
Problem. Nobody outside the system knows what a kilometre of concrete road, a public toilet block or a metre of drain should cost, so nobody can tell whether a tender is unusual.

What residents get. A typical cost range per unit for common works, built from the city's own tenders, and a marker on any tender far outside the range, with the reasons a tender can legitimately differ.

Data. Tender values and quantities from Mahatenders detail pages and bill-of-quantity files; BMC's schedule of rates if obtainable.

How. The extractor pulls quantity and unit from each tender. Code computes cost per unit by work category and year. Outliers become case files that the Challenger reviews: wider road, utility shifting, night-only work and difficult sites all raise cost honestly.

First version. Weeks. Needs a few hundred tenders in one category to be meaningful.

Watch out. Comparing unlike works is the main risk. Publish the range and the method; treat an outlier as a question.

docs.title: 11. Mega Project Meter
docs.text:
Problem. A handful of projects take a large share of capital spending. Their costs and deadlines shift from one budget speech to the next and the earlier figures are forgotten.

What residents get. For each major project, a timeline of every stated cost and completion date, with the document each came from. One line at the top: "First announced at ₹X for completion in year A; now ₹Y for year B."

Data. Budget speeches across years, tender awards and news reports. All public text.

How. The same mechanism as the promise tracker: each statement is a dated Promise with RESTATES links, so drift is a query.

First version. Days, for five projects.

Watch out. Scope changes are real. Record them when a source states them.

docs.title: 12. Reserves and Borrowing Watch
docs.text:
Problem. The city has long held large deposits and now plans significant capital spending and new forms of borrowing. Whether that is sustainable is a question residents and their representatives rarely have figures for.

What residents get. A simple chart per year: deposits held, amount drawn for capital works, new borrowing, and committed future liabilities, each from the budget documents.

Data. Budget documents and the commissioner's speech.

How. A small set of Indicator observations per fiscal year. No agents needed beyond extraction.

First version. Days.

Watch out. This is finance, and easy to misread. Have someone with public finance experience review the definitions before publishing.

docs.title: 13. Dues Ledger
docs.text:
Problem. The city is owed large sums in property tax, water charges and other dues. Recovering them reduces the pressure on everyone else.

What residents get. Totals owed by category and ward, the trend, and, where the city itself has published a list of large defaulters, that list with its source.

Data. Budget documents for totals; the city's own published defaulter lists and press notes for names.

How. Indicator observations for totals; Dues nodes only for entries the city has officially published.

First version. Weeks.

Watch out. Republish only names the city has already made public, with the date, and remove them when dues are cleared. Many dues are under legal dispute; say so. Never list individual householders.

docs.title: Works: what is being built outside your door
docs.text: Ideas 14 to 22. Idea 2, Jawabdar, is in ../mumbai-civic-graph/04-jawabdar.md.

docs.title: 14. Work Coming to Your Street
docs.text:
Problem. Residents learn about a road or drain work when the barricades arrive. They do not know how long it will last, who is doing it, or when to complain that it has overrun.

What residents get. They save their address or drop a pin. They get a message when a tender touching that area is published, when it is awarded and to whom, when the completion date passes, and when a corrigendum changes the scope or dates. Each message carries the tender number and a link to the notice.

Data. Mahatenders listings, corrigenda, status and award records, and BMC tender notices. Already mapped in ../mumbai-civic-graph/07-tender-portals.md.

How. The intake desk extracts road and locality names from each tender and matches them to map geometry. A subscription is a saved area. When a Tender, Award or Corrigendum node is added or changes within it, a message is drafted from the graph facts.

First version. Days, for one ward, by WhatsApp broadcast or email.

Watch out. Location matching from free-text tender titles will sometimes be wrong; show the title so the resident can judge. Collection must respect the portal's captcha, so freshness depends on how often someone collects.

docs.title: 15. Site Board QR
docs.text:
Problem. Work sites are meant to display a board with the work's name, cost, contractor and dates. Boards are often missing, faded or out of date.

What residents get. A QR code at the site. Scanning it shows the live record: what is being built, the cost, the contractor, the due date, the responsible engineer's post, how to report a problem, and whether the work is on time.

Data. The works graph. The code itself needs someone to put it up.

How. Each Work has a stable public page. Two routes to the street: residents' groups print and fix a notice themselves for works in their lane, or the ward office adds the code to official boards as a pilot.

First version. Weeks. The page is quick; getting codes onto sites takes people.

Watch out. A resident-posted notice must say clearly that it is unofficial and link to the official source.

docs.title: 16. Monsoon Readiness
docs.text:
Problem. Every year drains are desilted and vulnerable spots prepared before the rains, and every year parts of the city flood. Reported completion percentages are hard to check.

What residents get. From March to June, a countdown per drain and per known flooding spot: the work tendered, the contractor, the reported progress, and photos from residents nearby. After the first heavy rain, the same map with where water actually stood.

Data. Desilting tenders and awards; the city's published progress figures and lists of flooding spots; residents' photos.

How. Each drain stretch is an Asset with Work and Milestone nodes. Citizen reports attach as evidence. The audit desk runs on a date: on 1 May, which works are behind. The comparison of claimed progress with residents' evidence is a case file the Challenger reviews.

First version. Weeks. Timing matters: build before March to be useful that year.

Watch out. Flooding has causes beyond desilting, including tide and rainfall intensity. Report what was done and what happened; do not claim cause.

docs.title: 17. Dig Watch
docs.text:
Problem. A newly surfaced road is dug up for a cable or pipe and left patched badly. Residents cannot tell who dug, whether they had permission, or who must restore the surface.

What residents get. For a trench: the utility, the permission, the dates allowed, the restoration deadline and who is responsible for it.

Data. Trench permissions issued by the city. Not published in usable form as far as I know. Needs the roads department's cooperation or RTI.

How. (Utility)-[:GRANTED]->(TrenchPermission)-[:ON]->(Asset) with dates. Until permissions are available, residents' reports alone build a record of how often each road is dug and how long trenches stay open.

First version. Months for the full idea. The resident-report version is quick but answers less.

Watch out. Without permission data this can only say "this road was dug five times", not who was at fault.

docs.title: 18. Pothole Ledger
docs.text:
Problem. The same potholes return after every monsoon. Each is treated as a new complaint, so the pattern, and the contractor who built the road, never enter the picture.

What residents get. A history per road: every pothole reported, when it was fixed, how long the fix lasted. If the road is inside a contractor's defect liability period, a clear statement of that and a complaint that asks for repair at the contractor's cost.

Data. Residents' reports to start; the city's own pothole complaint data if it can be obtained; works and liability periods from the graph.

How. Complaint nodes attach to Asset. Repeat counts and time-to-fix are computed in code. The liability join is the same as Jawabdar's.

First version. Weeks. Useful once one monsoon's reports are in.

Watch out. Duplicate reports of the same pothole must be merged, by location and date, before counting.

docs.title: 19. Safety List
docs.text:
Problem. The city publishes a list of dangerously dilapidated buildings before each monsoon and has audited its bridges since the 2019 footbridge collapse. The lists exist as documents; few residents know whether their building or the bridge they cross is on one, or what was promised.

What residents get. A map and a search by address. For a listed building: its category, the date listed, what the notice requires. For a bridge: its last audit result, the repair or rebuild promised, the tender and the deadline.

Data. Published building lists and bridge audit summaries; bridge repair tenders.

How. Asset nodes of type building and bridge with Inspection results and linked Work. Year-on-year comparison shows buildings that stay on the list without action.

First version. Days, for the current year's list in one ward.

Watch out. A listing has consequences for residents' homes and can be disputed. Show the official record with its date and say how to check or contest it. Do not add anything the city has not published.

docs.title: 20. Hoarding Check
docs.text:
Problem. After the Ghatkopar hoarding collapse in 2024, the safety and legality of large hoardings became a public concern. A passer-by cannot tell whether a hoarding is licensed or who answers for it.

What residents get. Photograph a hoarding, give its location, and see whether a licence is on record, for what size, and which agency's land it stands on.

Data. The city's licence records, and those of other landowning agencies. Publication is uneven; likely needs RTI or cooperation.

How. (Licence)-[:FOR]->(Hoarding)-[:ON_LAND_OF]->(Agency). Residents' photos build an inventory of what stands on the street to compare with what is licensed.

First version. Weeks, once any licence list is in hand.

Watch out. "No record found" is not "illegal"; the records may be incomplete. Word it as a question to the licensing office.

docs.title: 21. Toilet Audit
docs.text:
Problem. Public and community toilets matter most to those with least, especially women and slum residents. Many are built and then closed, charging more than allowed, or without water.

What residents get. A map of toilets with who operates each, what the city paid to build or maintain it, the approved charge, and its current state as rated by users.

Data. Construction and maintenance tenders; operator agreements, probably by RTI; ratings from users.

How. Asset of type toilet, linked to Work, Contract and operator. A short rating by voice note or three taps. A toilet with a maintenance contract and repeated "closed" reports becomes a case for the ward office.

First version. Weeks, with a community group doing the first survey of one area.

Watch out. Partner with an organisation already working in the area; ratings need local trust to be honest and safe to give.

docs.title: 22. Reserved Plots Tracker
docs.text:
Problem. The development plan reserves plots for schools, hospitals, markets and parks. Many reservations go unbuilt for decades or are quietly changed.

What residents get. Every reserved plot in their ward on a map: what it is reserved for, whether the land has been acquired, whether anything is budgeted or tendered, and any change to the reservation.

Data. Development plan maps and reservation lists; budget lines for land acquisition; change notices.

How. (Reservation)-[:ON]->(Plot) with purpose and status, linked to Allocation and Work. Changes are dated edges, so a deleted reservation leaves a visible history.

First version. Months. Digitising plan sheets for even one ward is real work.

Watch out. Land status is legally complex and often in litigation. Report the plan and the budget; avoid statements about ownership.

docs.title: Services: what the money is supposed to buy
docs.text:
Ideas 23 to 28. Idea 5, Ward Lens, is in ../mumbai-civic-graph/05-ward-lens.md.

Service ideas are the most valuable to residents and the hardest to build, because the data sits inside hospitals, schools and depots and is rarely published. Each one needs a partner inside or close to the service. None is a hackathon-day build.

docs.title: 23. Hospital Watch
docs.text:
Problem. The city runs major hospitals and a network of smaller ones, with a large health budget. Patients meet long queues, unfilled posts, and scanners that are out of order for months.

What residents get. Per hospital: the budget, sanctioned and filled posts by category, beds, and the status of major equipment, with procurement and repair tenders linked. A notice when a machine a patient needs is reported out of service, and where the nearest working one is.

Data. Budget documents and equipment tenders are public. Vacancies and equipment status need RTI, questions raised in the corporation, or a partner such as a patients' group or resident doctors' association.

How. Asset of type hospital with Equipment, Post and Indicator nodes. The promise tracker covers announced beds and machines. Reports from patients and staff are citizen-tier evidence.

First version. Months. A narrow start is possible: track only announced new beds and machines against tenders, from public documents.

Watch out. No patient data, ever. Reports about staff must be about posts and vacancies, not individuals.

docs.title: 24. School Delivery Tracker
docs.text:
Problem. The city supplies its school pupils with uniforms, books, bags and devices. Deliveries have often arrived months into the school year.

What residents get. Per item and per year: when the tender was issued, when it was awarded, the promised delivery date, and when parents and teachers say the items actually arrived.

Data. Tenders and awards are public. Delivery dates need parents, teachers or school management committees to report.

How. Each item is a Work with milestones. A simple report from a parent ("received", "not yet") attaches to the school. The audit desk compares tender dates across years to show whether the process starts early enough to deliver by the first day of term.

First version. Weeks for the tender timeline; a school term for delivery reports.

Watch out. Work with a parents' or teachers' network. Reports should name the school, never the child.

docs.title: 25. Water Ledger
docs.text:
Problem. Supply hours vary sharply across the city, leaks run for days, and contamination complaints recur in the same lanes.

What residents get. Per locality: announced supply cuts, leak and contamination reports with time to repair, and the water works tendered for the area. A history that shows whether a lane's problem is new or chronic.

Data. Cut announcements and tenders are public. Leak, pressure and contamination records are internal; start with residents' reports.

How. Pipelines and reservoirs as Asset, complaints attached by location, works linked. Chronic clusters are found by counting in code.

First version. Months.

Watch out. Contamination reports are health claims. Label them as reported, encourage testing, and route them to the responsible office quickly.

docs.title: 26. Waste Contract Watch
docs.text:
Problem. Collection, transport and dump-site clearing are large recurring contracts, typically paid by weight or trips. Residents see only whether their bin was emptied.

What residents get. Per ward: who holds the collection contract, its value and terms, and residents' record of missed collections. For dump-site clearing: the contracted quantity, the reported progress and the deadline.

Data. Contracts via tenders and committee approvals. Weighbridge and trip data are internal.

How. Contract nodes with payment basis; Complaint nodes for missed collections; Milestone for clearing targets.

First version. Months. The contract map alone is quicker and already informative.

Watch out. Without weighbridge data, do not imply payments are wrong; show what is contracted and what residents report.

docs.title: 27. BEST Fleet Meter
docs.text:
Problem. Bus numbers are announced regularly: new electric buses, leased buses, fleet targets. Commuters experience longer waits. The city also pays a substantial subsidy to the undertaking each year.

What residents get. A timeline of every fleet announcement with its date and target, against the fleet size reported at later dates, and the annual subsidy from the civic budget.

Data. Budget documents, the undertaking's own statements and tenders, and news reports. BEST also tenders on Mahatenders.

How. The promise tracker's mechanism, with fleet size as a dated Indicator.

First version. Days.

Watch out. Distinguish owned from leased buses and buses on the books from buses in service, as the sources do.

docs.title: 28. Stalled Rehab Tracker
docs.text:
Problem. Families moved out for redevelopment are promised a new home and rent in the meantime. Projects stall for years and rent stops. This affects a very large number of households.

What residents get. For a project: the developer, the approvals and dates on record, the stated completion date, and reports from residents on rent arrears. A drafted complaint to the right authority.

Data. The slum rehabilitation and housing authorities publish some project information. Rent arrears come from residents.

How. A further Agency in the ontology; Project, Developer, Approval nodes; resident reports as evidence.

First version. Months.

Watch out. This sits outside the civic budget and largely outside BMC, so it stretches the challenge. It is also contested and often in court. Work with a housing rights group, publish only records and residents' own statements, and take legal advice.

docs.title: Accountability: making the system answer
docs.text: Ideas 29 to 36. Idea 3, Vachan Tracker, and idea 4, Thekedar Graph, are in ../mumbai-civic-graph/.

docs.title: 29. Committee Digest
docs.text:
Problem. Most spending decisions are approved in committee meetings, chiefly the Standing Committee. Agendas are long, formal and partly in Marathi. Few people outside read them.

What residents get. A weekly digest: each proposal approved, the amount, the contractor, the ward, and anything unusual such as a cost revision or an award to a sole bidder. Filterable by ward. Sent to subscribers and reporters.

Data. Committee agendas and resolutions. Availability online varies; confirm how to obtain them each week.

How. The intake desk reads each agenda item into Award and Contract facts, linking to tenders already in the graph. The drafter writes the digest. This is also the missing source of award data for the money trail.

First version. Days, for one meeting's agenda.

Watch out. A proposal on the agenda is not yet approved. Record the stage precisely.

docs.title: 30. RTI Commons
docs.text:
Problem. Thousands of right-to-information requests are filed about the same things. Each reply reaches one person and is lost. Many applications are rejected for being vague, and few people file a first appeal.

What residents get. A searchable library of RTI replies others have received. A drafting helper that asks for specific records in the form offices cannot easily refuse. A tracker for the thirty-day reply period, with a first appeal drafted automatically when it lapses.

Data. Replies contributed by residents and activists. No agency's permission is needed.

How. Each reply is a SourceDocument read by the intake desk, with personal details of the applicant removed. Facts from replies enter the graph at official tier. The gaps file from the audit desk supplies ready questions.

First version. Days. Seed it with replies that local activists already hold.

Watch out. Remove applicants' names and addresses before publishing. Check replies for third-party personal data.

docs.title: 31. Complaint Closure Audit
docs.text:
Problem. A complaint is marked resolved while the problem remains. The city's figures then show a high resolution rate.

What residents get. After a complaint is closed, a prompt: is it fixed? If not, a photo reopens it with evidence and adds it to a public count per ward and department of closures that residents dispute.

Data. Residents' own complaint numbers and photos. Official complaint data would improve it but is not required.

How. Complaint nodes with the official status and the resident's status side by side. The disputed share is computed per ward office and department.

First version. Days.

Watch out. Photos need location and time to count. Guard against one person filing many disputes by weighting per reporter.

docs.title: 32. Audit Para Tracker
docs.text:
Problem. The city's own auditor and the national auditor write reports listing specific irregularities. The national auditor's special audit of BMC works was tabled in 2023. After the headlines, nobody records what happened to each finding.

What residents get. Each audit observation as a card: what the auditor found, the amount involved, the department, the reply on record, and its status: answered, action taken, or silent. Counted by department.

Data. Published audit reports and any action-taken replies. RTI for the rest.

How. (AuditObservation)-[:ABOUT]->(Work|Contract|Department), linked to works in the graph where they can be matched. Each silent observation generates a drafted RTI and a question for the relevant committee.

First version. Days, for one report.

Watch out. An audit observation is the auditor's view, sometimes contested by the department. Quote it as such.

docs.title: 33. Court Order Compliance
docs.text:
Problem. The High Court has repeatedly directed the city on potholes, open manholes, footpaths, hoardings and air quality. Compliance is reviewed only when the case next comes up.

What residents get. Each direction as a plain statement with its date and deadline, the city's stated compliance, and residents' evidence for or against. Lawyers appearing in these matters get an organised record.

Data. Court orders are public. Compliance affidavits are filed in court and are harder to obtain.

How. (Direction)-[:FROM]->(Order) with deadline and responsible agency, linked to assets and works. The promise tracker's status rules apply.

First version. Weeks. Needs a lawyer to select and read the orders correctly.

Watch out. Do not comment on pending matters beyond what the orders say. Have a lawyer review every summary.

docs.title: 34. Corporator Report Card
docs.text:
Problem. Residents vote for a corporator and then have little way to see what they did: attendance, questions raised, proposals moved, funds used.

What residents get. A page per corporator from official records, updated as meetings happen, comparable across wards.

Data. Meeting proceedings and attendance records, likely by RTI or from civil society groups that already compile annual report cards. Fund use from idea 8.

How. Person, Post, Meeting, Question nodes. Counting only; no scores invented.

First version. Weeks.

Watch out. Apply identical measures to every corporator and publish the method. Offer each a right to correct their record.

docs.title: 35. Affidavit Explorer
docs.text:
Problem. Candidates file sworn declarations of assets, liabilities and pending cases at election time. They are public but scattered as scanned forms.

What residents get. Each representative's own declarations, searchable and comparable between elections.

Data. Election affidavits published by the election authorities; civil society groups already digitise many.

How. Extracted as Declaration facts attached to Person, each quoted from the affidavit.

First version. Days, for the corporators of one ward.

Watch out. Present declarations exactly as sworn, with no inference. Linking a representative to a contractor is a different, sensitive exercise that belongs under the review rules of the contractor graph and needs legal sign-off.

docs.title: 36. Ward Participatory Budget
docs.text:
Problem. Residents are consulted, if at all, after decisions are made. Small local works are chosen without them.

What residents get. Before the budget, residents of a ward propose small works, see rough costs from the rate card, and rank them. The ranked list goes to the corporator and ward committee. Afterwards, each chosen work is tracked to completion.

Data. Residents' proposals; costs from tender history.

How. Proposal nodes with support counts, linked to a Work if adopted. The city's existing residents' groups are natural organisers.

First version. Months, and only with a corporator or ward office willing to commit a share of discretionary funds.

Watch out. Online voting favours those already online and organised. Pair it with meetings in the ward, and verify that participants live there.

docs.title: Access and adoption
docs.text: Ideas 37 to 40. These are not separate products. They decide whether any of the other ideas reaches the people who need it and survives after the event.

docs.title: 37. Voice Line
docs.text:
Problem. Many of the residents with most at stake do not read English, are not comfortable with apps, or share a phone. A website does not reach them.

What residents get. A phone number and a WhatsApp number. Speak in Marathi or Hindi: "Who is responsible for the broken drain in our lane?" Hear the answer, and receive the drafted complaint as a message that can be forwarded or printed at a nearby shop.

How. Speech-to-text in front of the citizen desk agent and text-to-speech behind it. The agent already replies in the resident's language and asks for a location when it lacks one. Speech services are separate products to choose and test for Marathi quality.

First version. Weeks. WhatsApp voice notes first; a call-in line later.

Watch out. Test with real speakers from the areas served; accents and place names are where transcription fails. Always read back the location heard before answering.

docs.title: 38. Newsroom Feed
docs.text:
Problem. Local reporters, especially in Marathi papers, cover civic affairs with little time and no data desk. A finding that is never reported changes nothing.

What reporters get. A weekly brief: the largest awards, works that passed their deadline, allocations with nothing tendered, audit findings still unanswered. Each item has its documents attached and a note of what is not known.

How. The audit desk's ward brief, across all wards, with the Challenger's review included so reporters see the counter-argument up front.

First version. Days, once any audit output exists.

Watch out. Give it to all outlets on the same terms. Mark clearly what is official record and what is residents' report.

docs.title: 39. Open Publishing Kit
docs.text:
Problem. Everything here depends on reading PDFs after the fact. That is fragile and always late. The lasting fix is for the city to publish tenders, awards, works and payments as data.

What the city gets. A small, documented format based on the open contracting standard and the civic ontology; a validator; and a converter from the fields its systems already hold. Departments report once, at source, and stop answering the same questions by letter.

How. The ontology and validation shapes already written for the graph become the specification. A pilot with one department and one ward demonstrates it.

First version. Months, and only with the city's IT department as a partner.

Watch out. This is the adoption conversation, not a build. Lead with what it saves the city, and offer the tools built at the event as proof that the data is used.

docs.title: 40. Public Data Service
docs.text:
Problem. One team cannot build every tool the city needs. Others, including students, newsrooms and residents' associations, could build their own if the data were reachable.

What builders get. The civic graph as an open, read-only service: a documented API, bulk downloads under an open licence, and a tool interface that AI assistants can query directly with sources returned for every fact.

How. The read-only graph tools already defined for the agents, hosted behind rate limits. The same service backs the scheduled, unattended agent runs described in the multi-agent plan.

First version. Weeks after the graph is stable.

Watch out. Publish only official-tier and reviewed data in bulk. Keep residents' reports and anything under review out of downloads.

docs.title: Idea 41: Ek Plot, Ek Record
docs.text:
One plot, one record: a shared, neutral register of redevelopment approvals across BMC and SRA, built around the people both authorities are meant to serve.

Written 15 November 2026 in response to the BMC and SRA dispute over who approves redevelopment schemes on non-slum plots.

docs.title: The news, as reported
docs.text:
Facts below are from two press reports dated early November 2026. I could not open the underlying letters or the regulation text, so treat every item as "reported" until checked against the documents.

Date Event August 2024 The then municipal commissioner raises concerns about SRA approving schemes on plots without slums. 15 October 2024 The state Urban Development Department (UDD) issues directions on Regulation 33(11). BMC reads them as limiting the regulation to slum rehabilitation schemes. 22 July 2026 The BMC Commissioner writes to UDD, flags about 300 SRA-approved schemes, and asks that planning authority for these rest with the corporation. 2 September 2026 SRA replies, defending its use of the regulation. 2 November 2026 UDD writes to SRA reiterating that 33(11) proposals are to be processed by SRA under the October 2024 directions. It does not give BMC the planning powers it asked for.

What the regulation is for. Regulation 33(11) of the Development Control and Promotion Regulations 2034 lets schemes create permanent transit camp (PTC) tenements: homes for people displaced by infrastructure and redevelopment works. A newer provision, 33(20)(B), is reported as the route BMC would handle.

The two positions.

BMC SRA Reading 33(11) is for slum rehabilitation; it should not be used on vacant plots with no slum 33(11) exists to produce transit tenements and allows eligible plots to be pooled Concern Concessions meant for slums reach non-slum plots; premium revenue is lost; open space in prime areas shrinks Premiums are payable at standard rates under BMC policy; pooling reduces dependence on government land Asks Planning authority for these schemes Continue as directed by the state

The numbers in play (SRA figures as reported): 522 approved schemes; 32,337 tenements for project-affected people generated; 6,604 handed over; about 50,000 needed now and 2.2 lakh under the Development Plan. BMC's development charges were reported at nearly ₹12,000 crore in 2025-26, its second-largest revenue source.

The latest reports describe the disagreement as continuing. Developers quoted in them welcome the clarification but speak of hope, not of a settled process.

docs.title: Why this is a citizens' problem, not only a turf war
docs.text:
The dispute is argued in terms of powers and premiums. Four groups of residents carry the cost.

  1. Displaced families waiting for a home. By the reported figures, about 25,700 tenements have been generated on paper but not handed over. Nobody outside can see which schemes owe them or why they are late.
  2. Residents of buildings and slums under redevelopment. When two authorities contest a file, it slows. Families living on transit rent pay for every month of delay.
  3. Every taxpayer. If premiums are being forgone, that is public money. If they are not, the claim should be put to rest. Today neither side's figures can be checked.
  4. Neighbours. One authority approves the floor space; the other must supply the water, sewers, roads and open space. Nobody adds up what has been approved in a ward against what the ward can carry.

A fifth cost falls on everyone: when something goes wrong in such a building, a resident does not know which authority to approach, and each can point to the other.

docs.title: The solution in one paragraph
docs.text:
Do not try to decide who is right. Build the record that both authorities, the state and residents are missing: for every plot in a contested scheme, one page showing its status (slum or not, and on whose word), the scheme and regulation, which authority issued each approval, the tenements owed and delivered, the premiums assessed and paid, and the infrastructure sign-offs. Add a jurisdiction card that states which authority is currently directed to process the plot, under which dated direction, and who contests it. Then let agents keep the record current, prepare a neutral brief that sets the two readings side by side with the exact text each relies on, and answer residents' questions.

The register turns an argument about powers into three questions that data can answer: how many transit homes have these schemes actually delivered, how much premium has been paid or waived, and how much extra load has each ward been given.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
File Contents 01-solution-design.md Modules, ontology extension, jurisdiction rules, data sources, example queries 02-agents-and-pipeline.md The agents, how they fit the existing desks, and the LangGraph steps 03-implementation-plan.md Phases, hackathon slice, team, demo, risks, adoption

This builds on the foundation in ../../mumbai-civic-graph/: the same graph, the same agent desks and the same rule that every fact carries its source.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Maha Urban Development Dept clarifies DCR 33(11), Free Press Journal, 6 November 2026
  • BMC, SRA dispute over redevelopment approvals on non-slum plots, Realty Today
  • UDD reiterates directions on Regulation 33(11), Free Press Journal
  • BMC challenges SRA authority over non-slum land development, MSN (found in search; page did not load)
  • SRA publications: letters of intent under Regulation 33(11) (found in search; not opened)

docs.title: 1. Principles
docs.text:
• Neutral. The register records what each authority did and said. It does not rule on who has jurisdiction. Where the law is contested, it shows both readings and the direction currently in force.
  • Plot first. Everything hangs off the plot, identified by its city survey number, because that is the one thing both authorities, the land records and the homebuyers' regulator all share.
  • Sourced and dated. Every status, approval and figure carries its document, page, quote and date. A plot's slum status in particular is recorded as "declared by X on date Y", never as a bare fact.
  • Not legal advice. The jurisdiction card tells a resident where their file is and which office to approach. It says plainly that it is a summary of published directions.

docs.title: 2.1 Scheme Register
docs.text:
Every scheme under Regulation 33(11), and the neighbouring routes it is confused with (33(10) slum rehabilitation, 33(20)(B)), with:

  • the plots it covers and each plot's status;
  • whether plots were pooled, and which are slum and which are not;
  • the developer;
  • each approval in order (letter of intent, intimation of approval, commencement certificate, occupation certificate), with the issuing authority and date;
  • floor space sanctioned, by component.

This alone answers a question nobody can answer today: of the roughly 300 schemes BMC flagged and the 522 SRA counts, which are which, where are they, and what stage are they at.

docs.title: 2.2 Jurisdiction Card
docs.text:
For any plot or scheme, a short card:

Plot CTS 123, Village X, Ward K/W
Status:        Non-slum (no declaration on record; source: … , as of …)
Scheme:        33(11), pooled with CTS 456 (declared slum, …)
Directed to:   SRA   under UDD directions of 15 Oct 2024, reiterated 2 Nov 2026
Contested by:  BMC   (Commissioner's letter of 22 Jul 2026)
Approvals:     LOI by SRA (date) · IOA by SRA (date) · water NOC by BMC pending since (date)
Approach:      SRA, [office], for the scheme · BMC ward office for water, sewer, road

The card is produced by rules, described in section 4. When a new direction or court order arrives, the rule changes and every card updates, with the old answer kept in history.

docs.title: 2.3 Tenement Ledger
docs.text:
For each scheme: transit and project-affected tenements owed, built, handed over, and to whom. Rolled up by ward, developer and year.

This is the module with the most direct value to residents. The reported gap between tenements generated (32,337) and handed over (6,604) becomes a list of named schemes, each with its due date and current stage. A displaced family, or the agency responsible for housing them, can see which schemes near them owe homes.

docs.title: 2.4 Concession Meter
docs.text:
For each scheme: each premium or charge, the basis clause, the amount assessed, the amount paid, any concession and the clause that grants it.

BMC says premium revenue is being lost. SRA says premiums are payable at standard rates. The meter does not take a side. It shows, scheme by scheme, what was assessed and paid, and the total. If data from one authority is missing, the meter says so and names the record that would fill it.

docs.title: 2.5 Ward Load Sheet
docs.text: Per ward: additional built-up area approved, by authority and by regulation, against published figures for open space, water supply and sewer capacity where they exist. Shows whether approvals from two authorities are being added together by anyone.

docs.title: 2.6 Handoff Tracker
docs.text: Even where SRA is the planning authority, schemes need BMC sign-offs for water, sewerage, storm drains, roads and fire safety. Each is recorded with the date requested and the date issued. Median waiting time by department and ward shows where files actually stall, which is useful to both authorities and to the state.

docs.title: 2.7 Resident's Front Door
docs.text: Through the existing citizen desk: "Which authority has my building's file? What stage is it at? Who do I approach about transit rent, about water, about the occupation certificate?" Answered from the register, with sources, in Marathi, Hindi or English, with a drafted letter to the right office.

docs.title: 2.8 Dual-Reading Brief
docs.text: A neutral document for the state, the press and the public: the text of the regulation and each direction, BMC's reading and SRA's reading side by side with the exact words each relies on, the points where they differ, and what the register's data shows on each disputed factual claim. Produced by agents, reviewed by a lawyer. See 02-agents-and-pipeline.md.

docs.title: 3. Ontology extension
docs.text: Added to the Mumbai Civic Ontology in ../../mumbai-civic-graph/00-shared-foundation.md.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
Land         Plot, PlotStatusClaim, Reservation
Scheme       Scheme, SchemeComponent, Developer, Society
Approval     Approval (LOI, IOA, CC, OC), NOC, Authority (BMC, SRA, UDD, MHADA…)
Law          Regulation, Clause, Direction (government resolution, letter, circular),
             CourtOrder, Position, JurisdictionRule
Obligation   TenementObligation, Handover, Premium, Concession
People       ProjectAffectedGroup (never individuals)

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
(Scheme)-[:COVERS]->(Plot)                    (Scheme)-[:UNDER]->(Regulation)
(Scheme)-[:POOLED_WITH]->(Scheme)             (Developer)-[:PROMOTES]->(Scheme)
(PlotStatusClaim {status, as_of})-[:ABOUT]->(Plot)
(PlotStatusClaim)-[:MADE_BY]->(Authority)
(Approval {kind, date})-[:FOR]->(Scheme)      (Authority)-[:ISSUED]->(Approval)
(NOC {dept, requested_on, issued_on})-[:FOR]->(Scheme)
(Direction {date})-[:INTERPRETS]->(Clause)    (Authority)-[:ISSUED]->(Direction)
(Direction)-[:REITERATES|SUPERSEDES]->(Direction)
(Position {date, summary})-[:TAKEN_BY]->(Authority)
(Position)-[:ON]->(Clause)                    (Position)-[:STATED_IN]->(SourceDocument)
(JurisdictionRule)-[:BASED_ON]->(Direction|CourtOrder)
(JurisdictionRule)-[:ASSIGNS]->(Authority)
(Scheme)-[:OWES]->(TenementObligation {count, kind, due_on})
(Handover {count, date})-[:AGAINST]->(TenementObligation)
(Premium {kind, assessed, paid})-[:FOR]->(Scheme)
(Premium)-[:PAYABLE_TO]->(Authority)
(Concession {amount})-[:ON]->(Premium)        (Concession)-[:GRANTED_UNDER]->(Clause)

PlotStatusClaim is deliberately a claim and not a property. Whether a plot is a slum is the heart of the dispute, and two authorities may say different things about the same plot at different times.

docs.title: 4. Jurisdiction rules
docs.text:
Rules are data, not code. Each has conditions, an outcome, a basis and a validity period.

- id: rule-33-11-udd-2024
  when:
    scheme.regulation: "33(11)"
  assigns: SRA
  basis: direction:udd-2024-10-15
  valid_from: 2024-10-15
  status: in_force
  reiterated_by: direction:udd-2026-11-02
  contested_by:
    - position: position:bmc-2026-07-22
      applies_when: "scheme covers a plot with no slum status claim"

Resolution is done in code:

  1. Collect the scheme's regulation and every plot's status claims.
  2. Select rules whose conditions match and whose validity covers today.
  3. Among directions, prefer the latest that has not been superseded; a court order outranks a direction.
  4. Return the assigned authority, the basis, and any position that contests it for this fact pattern.

The output always separates three things: what is directed, who contests it, and what is simply unknown. A lawyer on the team reviews every rule before it is used. The exact wording of each condition must come from the direction's text, which this plan has not seen.

docs.title: 5. Data sources
docs.text:
None of these was tested for this plan. Confirm each in a data spike.

Source Gives Likely access SRA website publications, including letters of intent issued under 33(11) Scheme, plots, developer, approvals, tenement counts Published lists and PDFs MahaRERA public project search Projects, promoter, survey numbers, planning authority named, approvals and dates Public website BMC online building proposal system Approvals and NOCs issued by BMC Public status lookup, if available; otherwise RTI DCPR 2034 text and amendments Regulation and clauses Published UDD directions and government resolutions Directions State resolutions portal; the letters themselves may need RTI Commissioner's and SRA's letters Positions Press reports now; RTI for the text Slum declarations and SRA slum mapping, including the SRA GIS portal at umd.nic.in/sra (slum areas by ward, cluster and hut id) Plot status claims, with the map layer as evidence Partly published; the GIS portal is interactive and needs SRA's agreement for a data export Development Plan 2034 sheets Reservations, open space Published maps Bombay High Court orders Court orders on jurisdiction and individual schemes Public BMC budget documents Premium and development charge revenue Published Residents' associations and housing rights groups Handover and transit rent status on the ground Partnership

Premium payments and NOC dates per scheme are the hardest to obtain and will probably need RTI to both authorities. The register should show these as named gaps from the first day, and the RTI drafter should produce the applications.

docs.title: 6. Example queries
docs.text:
Schemes that include a plot with no slum status claim, by ward:

MATCH (s:Scheme)-[:UNDER]->(:Regulation {code: '33(11)'})
MATCH (s)-[:COVERS]->(p:Plot)-[:LOCATED_IN]->(w:AdminWard)
OPTIONAL MATCH (c:PlotStatusClaim {status: 'slum'})-[:ABOUT]->(p)
WITH s, w, p, count(c) AS slum_claims
WHERE slum_claims = 0
RETURN w.code, count(DISTINCT s) AS schemes, count(DISTINCT p) AS plots
ORDER BY schemes DESC

Tenements owed and not yet handed over, largest first:

MATCH (s:Scheme)-[:OWES]->(o:TenementObligation)
OPTIONAL MATCH (h:Handover)-[:AGAINST]->(o)
WITH s, o, sum(h.count) AS handed
RETURN s.name, o.count AS owed, handed, o.count - handed AS outstanding, o.due_on
ORDER BY outstanding DESC
LIMIT 50

Where sign-offs wait longest:

MATCH (n:NOC)-[:FOR]->(:Scheme)-[:COVERS]->(:Plot)-[:LOCATED_IN]->(w:AdminWard)
WHERE n.issued_on IS NULL
RETURN w.code, n.dept, count(n) AS pending, min(n.requested_on) AS oldest
ORDER BY pending DESC

Premiums assessed against paid, by receiving authority:

MATCH (pr:Premium)-[:FOR]->(s:Scheme)
MATCH (pr)-[:PAYABLE_TO]->(a:Authority)
OPTIONAL MATCH (c:Concession)-[:ON]->(pr)
RETURN a.name, sum(pr.assessed) AS assessed, sum(pr.paid) AS paid, sum(c.amount) AS concessions

sum over an empty optional match should be checked on the chosen database; compute the difference in code if it returns null.

docs.title: Agents and pipeline
docs.text: This idea reuses the three desks in ../../mumbai-civic-graph/08-multi-agent-system.md and adds one: a Regulation desk. Nothing here has been built or run.

docs.title: 1. What each desk does for this idea
docs.text: Desk Existing role Added for this idea Intake Reads documents into verified facts Reads letters of intent, approval letters, RERA project pages and handover records into Scheme, Plot, Approval, TenementObligation, Premium facts Regulation (new) Reads regulations, directions and letters into Clause, Direction, Position facts and drafts jurisdiction rules; writes the dual-reading brief Audit Finds overdue works and gaps Finds overdue tenement handovers, schemes with a non-slum plot and no stated basis, sign-offs pending longest, missing premium records Citizen Answers residents from the graph Gains a which_authority tool that returns the jurisdiction card

docs.title: 2. The Regulation desk
docs.text:
Four agents. The lead coordinates; two advocates each argue one authority's reading; a rule drafter turns the texts into candidate rules.

Agent Model Job Tools Regulation lead Claude Opus 5.5 Plans the reading, delegates, writes the neutral brief, reconciles the advocates' points Files; read-only graph tools Rule drafter Claude Sonnet 5.5 From each regulation and direction, extracts conditions and outcomes as candidate JurisdictionRule records, each with the clause and quote it rests on Files only BMC-reading advocate Claude Sonnet 5.5 Makes the strongest case for the corporation's reading, from the texts only Files only SRA-reading advocate Claude Sonnet 5.5 Makes the strongest case for the authority's reading, from the texts only Files only

The two advocates use the same agent definition with a different brief, so neither is favoured by its instructions. The definition would be added to managed-agents/agents/ in the same file format as the existing agents, and the lead would list the drafter and the advocate in its roster.

docs.title: Instructions that matter
docs.text:
For the advocates:

Argue only from the documents you are given. Quote the exact words you rely on, with document and page. Do not characterise the other side's motives. Where the text is silent or ambiguous, say so; that is a finding, not a weakness. End with the three factual questions which, if answered by data, would most help or hurt this reading.

For the lead:

You do not decide who is right. Set out the text, then each reading with its quotes, then where they differ and why. For each disputed factual claim, state what the register's data shows and what it cannot show. Use the same length and tone for both readings. Do not use words that imply bad faith. A lawyer will review this before anyone else sees it.

For the rule drafter:

A rule may contain only conditions the text states. If a condition needs interpretation, write it as a contested condition and name the position that contests it. Never write a rule from a press report.

docs.title: Why two advocates and not one summary
docs.text:
A single summary of a legal dispute tends to drift toward whichever side's documents are longer or more recent. Two agents with equal briefs and equal sources, followed by a lead held to equal length and tone, is a cheap structural guard against that. The advocates' closing lists of factual questions also become the audit desk's work list.

This adds three agents' worth of tokens per brief. A brief is written once per new direction or order, not per resident's question, so the cost is small and bounded by the session budget.

docs.title: 3. Outcome rubric for the brief (starter)
docs.text:
• The brief quotes the operative text of Regulation 33(11) and of each direction, with document and page.
  • Each reading is stated in its own section of comparable length, and every assertion in it is tied to a quote.
  • A table lists each point of difference with the words each side relies on.
  • Each disputed factual claim (premium loss, schemes on vacant plots, tenements delivered) is followed by what the register shows, with counts and sources, or the statement that the register holds no data on it.
  • The brief does not state or imply which reading is correct.
  • No sentence attributes motive or bad faith to an authority, an officer or a developer.
  • A final section lists the records that would settle each factual claim and which authority holds them.

docs.title: 4. Pipeline
docs.text:
Added to the LangGraph pipeline in managed-agents/orchestrator.py as a second entry point.

new document (direction, letter, court order, LOI list)
        │
        ▼
   classify ── scheme document ──► intake ──► quote check and load ──► audit (tenements, sign-offs)
        │                                                                   │
        └── legal text ──► regulation desk: extract clauses and positions   │
                                   │                                        │
                                   ▼                                        │
                         draft rules ──► LAWYER REVIEWS RULES (pause)       │
                                   │                                        │
                                   ▼                                        │
                         recompute jurisdiction cards (code)                │
                                   │                                        │
                                   ├──► cards that changed ──► notify subscribers
                                   ▼                                        ▼
                         dual-reading brief ──────────────► EDITOR OR LAWYER RELEASES (pause)
                                                                            │
                                                                            ▼
                                                                         publish

Two points are fixed in code and not left to a model:

  • Rules do not take effect until a lawyer approves them. The pipeline pauses with the candidate rules and their quotes. Until then, cards show the previous answer with a banner that a new direction is under review.
  • Cards are computed by code from approved rules. No agent writes a jurisdiction answer.

When a new direction arrives, as on 2 November 2026, the visible result is: every affected card shows the new basis and date, subscribers are told what changed for their plot, and the brief gains a section.

docs.title: 5. The which_authority tool
docs.text:
Added to the citizen desk's tools.

Input Output A plot's survey number, or a location, or a scheme or society name Plot status claims with sources; scheme and regulation; authority currently directed to process it and the basis; any position contesting that; approvals and pending sign-offs; which office to approach for which matter

The citizen desk is told to present the directed authority and the contest as two separate facts, and to add that this summarises published directions and is not legal advice.

docs.title: 6. Safeguards specific to this idea
docs.text: Risk Control The tool is seen as taking a side Equal-brief advocates; rubric on balance; both authorities offered a right to correct the record before release A wrong jurisdiction answer misdirects a resident Rules approved by a lawyer; every card shows its basis and date; "under review" banner when the law moves A plot is wrongly shown as slum or non-slum Status is always a dated claim attributed to its maker; conflicting claims are shown together Displaced families are identified Tenement records are counts per scheme. No names, no allotment lists. A developer is implied to be at fault for a delay Record stages and dates only; the Challenger reviews any case file naming a developer The matter is before a court Report orders as issued; no comment on pending proceedings

docs.title: 1. Phases
docs.text:
Phase Work Done when 0. Read the texts Obtain Regulation 33(11), 33(10) and 33(20)(B), the directions of 15 October 2024 and 2 November 2026, and, by RTI if needed, the two authorities' letters A lawyer on the team has read them and written a one-page note on what each actually says 1. Scheme Register Collect SRA's published 33(11) letters of intent and matching RERA project pages for one ward; extract schemes, plots, developers and approvals 20 to 30 schemes loaded, each fact quoted from its source 2. Plot status Attach slum declarations and survey references as status claims Every plot in the register has at least one claim or an explicit "no claim found" 3. Tenement Ledger Extract tenements owed from letters of intent; handovers from SRA publications and RTI Owed and handed-over counts reconcile, in total, with SRA's published figures for the schemes covered 4. Jurisdiction rules and cards Encode rules from the directions; lawyer review; card generator A card for every scheme, each with its basis 5. Regulation desk Advocates, rule drafter, lead; first dual-reading brief Brief passes its rubric and a lawyer's review 6. Resident's front door which_authority tool on the citizen desk; subscriptions for changes A resident's question about a real scheme is answered correctly, as checked by someone who knows the scheme 7. Concession Meter and Handoff Tracker RTI applications to both authorities for premium and sign-off records; ingest replies First replies loaded; gaps listed for the rest 8. Ward Load Sheet Sum approved floor space by ward and authority; add open space and service figures One ward complete

Phases 1 to 4 need only published documents. Phases 7 and 8 depend on records the authorities hold.

docs.title: 2. Hackathon slice
docs.text:
Aim for one ward and three things that work end to end.

Build Shows Scheme Register for 20 to 30 schemes, on a map "Here are the schemes behind the headline, in this ward" Tenement Ledger for those schemes "This many transit homes are owed here; this many have been handed over" Jurisdiction card for each, plus one dual-reading brief "Here is who is directed to handle each, on what basis, and what each side says"

Leave premiums, sign-offs and ward load as named gaps with drafted RTI applications. Showing the gap and the application that would fill it is part of the demo.

docs.title: Before the event
docs.text: Task Output Open the SRA publications page for 33(11) letters of intent and record what it actually contains Source note Look up five of those schemes on the RERA public search and note which fields are shown Field list Obtain the regulation text and both directions Documents in the archive Ask a lawyer to join the team A name Pick the ward One with several 33(11) schemes

docs.title: On the day
docs.text: Hours Work 0 to 1 Agree the demo. Lawyer reads the texts and writes the one-page note. 1 to 3 Intake of letters of intent and RERA pages for the ward. First ten schemes on a map. 3 to 5 Tenement counts. Jurisdiction rules encoded and reviewed. Cards generated. 5 to 6 Regulation desk produces the brief. Lawyer edits it. 6 to 7 Citizen desk answers three prepared questions in Marathi and English. Rehearse. 7 to 8 Pitch. Backup recording.

docs.title: 3. Team
docs.text:
Role Why essential Lawyer with development control experience Reads the regulation and directions correctly; approves rules and the brief Planner or architect who files proposals Knows what a letter of intent contains and how approvals sequence Data and graph engineer Register, rules engine, queries AI engineer Intake and Regulation desk agents, rubrics Front end Map, card, ledger Housing rights or residents' group contact Ground truth on handovers and transit rent

Without the lawyer, build only the Scheme Register and Tenement Ledger and leave the jurisdiction card out.

docs.title: 4. Demo script
docs.text:
1. Show the headline. "Two authorities, one regulation, about 300 schemes in question. Which ones? Where?"
  2. Open the map of one ward. Each scheme is a pin. Tap one: plots, status claims, regulation, approvals, each with its document.
  3. Show its jurisdiction card: directed to SRA under the state's directions, contested by BMC, with both dates.
  4. Open the Tenement Ledger for the ward: owed, handed over, outstanding, by scheme. "These are the transit homes the argument is supposed to be about."
  5. Open the dual-reading brief: both readings, same length, each with the words it relies on, then what the data shows.
  6. Ask the citizen desk, in Marathi: "Our building's redevelopment file is with which office, and whom do we ask about transit rent?"
  7. Show the gaps list and one drafted RTI application for premium records.
  8. Close: "We have not decided who is right. We have built the record that lets the state decide on evidence, and lets residents stop waiting in the dark."

docs.title: 5. Adoption
docs.text:
The natural owner is the state Urban Development Department, which both authorities answer to and which has now written twice on the same question.

Audience What they gain UDD One view of every scheme, both authorities' actions on it, and delivery against the regulation's purpose. Evidence for any future direction. SRA A public record of transit tenements delivered, which is its case for the regulation BMC Visibility of what has been approved in each ward by another authority, and of premiums due to it Displaced families and their representatives Which schemes owe homes, and when Residents in redevelopment Where their file is and who to approach Developers A predictable statement of which authority and which sign-offs apply

Offer it first as a joint pilot for one ward, with both authorities invited to correct their own records before anything is public. A register both have checked is worth more than one that either can dismiss.

docs.title: 6. Measures of success
docs.text:
• Share of the reported 522 schemes in the register with at least a letter of intent on file.
  • Share of tenement obligations with a known handover status.
  • Number of jurisdiction cards whose basis a lawyer has confirmed.
  • Median days a BMC sign-off has been pending, once that data exists.
  • Residents' questions answered with a source, and how many were corrected afterwards.
  • Whether either authority, or the department, asks for access.

docs.title: 7. Risks
docs.text: Risk Mitigation The texts say something different from the press reports Phase 0 comes first; nothing in the rules is taken from news Published SRA data is too thin to build the register Fall back to RERA project pages, which name the planning authority and approvals; state coverage honestly Survey numbers do not match across sources Keep each source's identifier and link them as claims; a planner reviews doubtful matches The state issues a new direction or a court rules mid-build The rules are data; add the document, review, and every card updates. This is the design working as intended. The project is used by one side against the other Equal treatment in the brief; right of correction for both; publish the method Legal exposure from naming developers Stages and dates only; Challenger and lawyer review; no characterisation Scope: this is partly outside the civic budget The link to the challenge is direct: premium revenue is public money, and transit homes are a public promise. Keep those two at the centre.

docs.title: 8. What this plan has not established
docs.text:
• The exact wording of Regulation 33(11), 33(20)(B) and the two directions.
  • Whether "generated" in SRA's tenement figures means sanctioned, under construction or built.
  • What SRA's publications page and the RERA search actually expose, and in what form.
  • Whether BMC publishes approval and sign-off status in a usable way.

Each of these is a task in "Before the event". The design holds whichever way they turn out, but the hackathon slice should be cut to fit what the data spike finds.

docs.title: Aamcha Hishob: the final recommendation
docs.text:
One knowledge graph of how Mumbai is governed, paid for and built, with an intelligence layer on top, so that every idea in this repository becomes a small application on a shared base and not a separate project.

Aamcha Hishob (आमचा हिशोब, "our account") is the public name. Hishob is the word a Mumbaikar uses when asking for an account of money: hishob dya, give the account. The name says whose money it is and what is being asked for. The technical name for the data layer underneath stays the civic knowledge graph.

Before using the name publicly, check that it is free as a trademark and as a domain; a quick web search on 15 November 2026 found no civic platform using it.

docs.title: The recommendation in brief
docs.text:
Stop choosing between ideas. The forty-one ideas in ../mumbai-civic-ideas/ ask the same few questions of the same few kinds of record: money, contracts, works, places, offices, people, rules and evidence. Build that record once, properly, and each idea is a query, a view or an agent on top of it.

The platform has five layers.

 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ 5  APPLICATIONS    alerts · money trail · who is responsible · ward brief ·  │
 │                    promise tracker · tenement ledger · newsroom feed · API   │
 ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ 4  INTELLIGENCE    Claude models · Managed Agents desks · LangGraph workflows│
 │                    intake · regulation · audit · steward · analyst · citizen │
 ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ 3  SEMANTIC AND    glossary (Marathi, Hindi, English) · metric definitions · │
 │    SEARCH          question routing · text + vector + graph retrieval ·      │
 │                    citations checked in code · access tiers                  │
 ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ 2  KNOWLEDGE       ten linked graphs under one ontology · every fact sourced,│
 │                    dated and tiered · rules as data                          │
 ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ 1  DATA            immutable archive of every source document · parsed text ·│
 │                    geometry · residents' reports · RTI replies               │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Why this is the right final idea
docs.text:
• It matches the shape of the problem. Accountability fails at the joins between records, not inside any one of them. A graph is a store of joins.
  • It compounds. Each new source improves every application. Tender data collected for street alerts also feeds the money trail, the contractor record and the ward brief.
  • It can start small and stay honest. One ward, four graphs and three applications is a real product. Coverage grows by source and by ward, and the platform always states what it does not hold.
  • It is adoptable. The same base serves residents, reporters, corporators, ward officers and the state. Officers gain from it, which is what makes a civic body take it up.
  • It survives the team. An open ontology, an open archive and an open API let others build on it.

docs.title: What it answers
docs.text:
Each line is a question the platform should answer with sources, in Marathi, Hindi or English.

Question Graphs used Where did the money for my road come from, who built it, and is it still under warranty? Money, Procurement, Works and Assets Who is responsible for this drain, and who is above them? Organisation and Jurisdiction, Works and Assets What was promised for my ward this year and what has started? Voice, Money, Procurement Which office has my building's redevelopment file? Land and Planning, Law and Oversight How much of the health budget was spent in each of the last five years? Money Which audit findings has nobody answered? Law and Oversight What has my corporator's fund been spent on? People and Representation, Money, Works and Assets Which works due before the monsoon are behind? Works and Assets, Procurement Which records do we not have, and who holds them? Evidence (gaps)

docs.title: Collection rules
docs.text:
• Archive every document before parsing it, with URL, time and hash. The archive is never edited.
  • Prefer a published file over a scraped page, and a request to the agency over both.
  • Do not defeat captchas or logins. A person collects those pages in a browser session at a slow rate, or the data is requested.
  • Check each publisher's terms before storing or republishing news text; store links and short quotes where terms require it.
  • Record the licence of every source and carry it through to anything published.
  • Remove personal details of private individuals at intake. The platform holds no patient, pupil, applicant or beneficiary names.

docs.title: 1. One ontology, ten graphs
docs.text:
The Mumbai Civic Ontology (MCO) is a single vocabulary. The ten graphs are modules of it that share places, organisations, time and evidence. A node belongs to one module; relationships cross modules freely, and those crossings are where the value is.

                         ┌───────────────┐
                         │   EVIDENCE    │  every node and edge points here
                         └───────┬───────┘
   ┌──────────┐  funds   ┌───────┴───────┐  executed as  ┌────────────────┐
   │  MONEY   ├─────────►│  PROCUREMENT  ├──────────────►│ WORKS & ASSETS │
   └────┬─────┘          └───────┬───────┘               └───────┬────────┘
        │ voted by               │ approved by                   │ located in / owned by
   ┌────┴─────────────┐  ┌───────┴────────┐              ┌───────┴────────┐
   │ PEOPLE &         │  │ ORGANISATION & │◄─────────────┤     PLACE      │
   │ REPRESENTATION   │  │ JURISDICTION   │  responsible └───────┬────────┘

docs.title: 2. Vocabularies reused
docs.text:
Need Standard Tenders, awards, contracts Open Contracting Data Standard concepts Organisations, posts, reporting W3C Organization Ontology People, memberships, elected bodies Popolo Provenance W3C PROV-O Geometry GeoSPARQL Hierarchies and glossaries SKOS Time OWL-Time Statistical observations RDF Data Cube Legal texts and their parts ELI-style identifiers for acts, regulations and clauses Datasets and licences DCAT

Where a standard has a term, MCO uses it or declares an equivalence. MCO adds only what Mumbai needs and the standards lack: wards, budget heads, defect liability, tenement obligations, jurisdiction rules.
