docs.title: 3.11 Evidence
docs.text: SourceDocument, Claim, Run, Correction, Gap. Every node and relationship in every other module carries source_id, page, quote, tier, confidence, valid_from, valid_to, extracted_by.

docs.title: 4. Four rules that hold everywhere
docs.text:
1. No source, no fact. A record without a document, page and quote is rejected at load.
  2. Tiers. official, reported, citizen, derived. Answers say which they rest on. Bulk downloads contain only official and reviewed data.
  3. Time. Nothing is overwritten. A changed deadline is a new dated edge; the old one keeps its valid_to. History is a query.
  4. Claims where facts are contested. Slum status, road ownership and jurisdiction are stored as dated claims attributed to whoever made them, never as bare properties.

docs.title: 5. Identity and entity resolution
docs.text:
Entity Primary key Fallback Tender Mahatenders id BMC bid number Budget head Budget code plus budget part Normalised name under its parent Contractor Registration number; company id Normalised name plus address, held as POSSIBLY_SAME_AS until reviewed Asset Own id linked to OpenStreetMap way id Name plus ward plus nearest landmark Plot Survey number plus village Geometry Person Office held plus term Never merged on name alone Document Content hash URL plus fetch time

Merges of organisations need a hard identifier or a reviewer's approval. Merges of people need an official identifier. Unsure pairs are linked, shown as unsure, and never used to raise a finding.

docs.title: 6. Authoring and validation
docs.text:
ontology/
  mco-core.ttl          classes and properties shared by all modules
  mco-money.ttl  mco-procurement.ttl  mco-works.ttl  mco-org.ttl  mco-people.ttl
  mco-land.ttl   mco-services.ttl     mco-voice.ttl  mco-law.ttl  mco-evidence.ttl
  shapes/               SHACL shapes, one file per module
  glossary.ttl          SKOS terms in Marathi, Hindi and English
  rules/                jurisdiction and status rules as YAML

A short example of the style:

mco:Tender a owl:Class ;
    rdfs:label "Tender"@en, "निविदा"@mr ;
    rdfs:comment "An invitation to bid for a work, supply or service."@en ;
    skos:closeMatch ocds:Tender .

mco:forWork a owl:ObjectProperty ;
    rdfs:domain mco:Tender ; rdfs:range mco:Work .

mco:TenderShape a sh:NodeShape ;
    sh:targetClass mco:Tender ;
    sh:property [ sh:path mco:tenderId ; sh:minCount 1 ; sh:maxCount 1 ] ;
    sh:property [ sh:path mco:estimatedCost ; sh:datatype xsd:integer ; sh:minInclusive 0 ] ;
    sh:property [ sh:path prov:wasDerivedFrom ; sh:minCount 1 ] .

From these files a build step generates: the record schema the extractor agents fill, the label and relationship whitelist the loader enforces, the validation run on every batch, and the public documentation. The ontology is versioned; each fact records the ontology version it was loaded under.

docs.title: 7. Physical stores
docs.text:
Store Holds Choice Property graph All ten graphs, for traversal On AWS: Neptune Database Serverless or Neo4j Community by profile, with HydraDB on trial; see architecture/adr/0004-graph-database.md Triple store The same data as linked open data, for publishing and SPARQL Apache Jena Fuseki or Oxigraph, fed by export Relational and spatial Geometry, subscriptions, review queues, metric tables Postgres with PostGIS Text and vector index Document passages and node summaries See 03-semantic-and-search-layer.md Object storage The immutable document archive Any S3-compatible store

HydraDB's README describes an OpenCypher subset with no built-in text or vector index, so search lives outside it, and every query the platform depends on must be checked against its compatibility notes. The triple store is not needed on the day; it becomes useful when the data is published for others.

docs.title: 8. Competency questions
docs.text:
The ontology is correct when these can be answered by a query. Use them as acceptance tests.

  1. For a given road, list every work in the last five years with contractor, cost, due date and liability end date.
  2. For a budget head and year, list works funded, tenders issued and the unspent remainder.
  3. For a point on the map, return the owning agency, responsible post and escalation chain.
  4. List contractors awarded a contract within twelve months after a recorded penalty.
  5. For a promise, list every restatement with its deadline, and the linked works.
  6. For a ward, list schemes that owe transit tenements, with owed and handed-over counts.
  7. For a plot, return every status claim with its maker and date.
  8. For an audit observation, return the work it concerns and any reply on record.
  9. For any fact shown to a user, return the document, page and quote.
  10. List every gap, the record that would close it, and the office that holds that record.

docs.title: Semantic and search layer
docs.text: The graph holds facts. This layer makes them findable, comparable and safe to show. It sits between the stores and the agents, and it is mostly ordinary software: the model is used where language is needed and nowhere else.

docs.title: 1. The semantic layer
docs.text: Three things, each defined once and used by every application and agent.

docs.title: 1.1 Glossary
docs.text:
A SKOS vocabulary of civic terms with labels in Marathi, Hindi and English, synonyms, abbreviations and the ontology class or property each maps to.

Term Also written as Maps to Standing Committee स्थायी समिती, SC Committee Defect liability period DLP, दोष दायित्व कालावधी, warranty DefectLiabilityPeriod K/West ward K/W, के पश्चिम, Andheri West ward AdminWard {code: 'K/W'} Storm water drain SWD, nullah, नाला Asset {type: 'drain'} Budget estimate BE, अर्थसंकल्पीय अंदाज Allocation.amount_be

The glossary drives query expansion, entity lookup, extraction prompts and the labels in every interface. Road and locality aliases confirmed by reviewers are added to it from the ward memory store.

docs.title: 1.2 Metrics
docs.text:
Each indicator is a small declarative definition compiled to a query. The scorecard, the agent and the export therefore return the same number.

metric: capital_utilisation
label: {en: "Share of capital budget spent", mr: "भांडवली खर्चाचे प्रमाण"}
numerator:   sum(Allocation.amount_actual) where BudgetHead.kind = 'capital'
denominator: sum(Allocation.amount_be)     where BudgetHead.kind = 'capital'
grain: [Department, FiscalYear]
unit: percent
tiers: [official]
caveats: "Actuals for the latest year are provisional until the next budget book."

Starter set: capital utilisation; share of allocation tendered; median days from tender to award; share of works past due; works under liability with open defects; tenements owed against handed over; complaints disputed after closure; audit observations unanswered.

Every metric carries its caveats, and an answer that uses a metric must repeat them.

docs.title: 1.3 Named views
docs.text: Common traversals with fixed, tested queries, exposed as tools: trace_money, who_is_responsible, work_status, scheme_card, ward_summary, contractor_record, promise_history, gaps_for. Agents call these first and write free-form queries only when no view fits.

docs.title: 2. Storage for search
docs.text:
Index Holds Used for Full-text Every archived page, in its original script, with transliteration; node names and aliases Exact numbers and names: tender ids, road names, contractor names Vector Passages of documents and one generated summary per ward, department, contractor, scheme and major work Questions phrased in everyday language, across languages Graph The ten graphs Multi-hop questions and anything about relationships Spatial Geometry of wards, roads, plots, assets "Near me", "in this ward", point lookups Metric tables Pre-computed metric values Comparisons and trends

A practical choice that keeps operations small: Postgres with its full-text search, the pgvector extension and PostGIS covers the text, vector, spatial and metric rows in one database. OpenSearch is the step up if volume demands it. The embedding model must handle Marathi and Hindi well; choose it by testing on real queries, not by reputation.

Passages are chunked by document structure (a tender's header data, a committee item, a budget table row) and each chunk keeps its document, page and the ids of the graph nodes extracted from it. That link is what lets retrieval move from a passage to the graph and back.

docs.title: 3. How a question is answered
docs.text:
question (any of three languages, text or transcribed voice)
   │
   ▼
1. Understand     normalise script, expand with glossary, find entities and places
   │
   ▼
2. Route          lookup · trail · metric · rule · exploratory
   │
   ├─ lookup        entity search ► node card
   ├─ trail         named view ► ordered facts
   ├─ metric        metric engine ► numbers with caveats
   ├─ rule          rules engine ► card with basis and contest
   └─ exploratory   text + vector retrieval ► expand through the graph from the
                    nodes those passages mention ► rerank
   │
   ▼
3. Compose        the agent writes the answer from the retrieved facts only
   │
   ▼
4. Check          code verifies every figure, date and name in the answer appears
                  in a retrieved fact, and attaches source, page and tier
   │
   ▼
5. Respond        answer, sources, what is not known, and how to find out

Routing is a cheap classification. Most residents' questions are lookups and trails, which never need open-ended retrieval; that keeps answers fast, cheap and reproducible. The exploratory path is for reporters and researchers.

docs.title: The exploratory path in more detail
docs.text:
1. Retrieve passages by text and by vector, and merge the two rankings.
  2. Collect the graph nodes those passages were extracted into.
  3. Expand one or two hops along relationships that matter for the question type (a tender's award and contractor; a work's asset and ward).
  4. Add the pre-written summaries of the wards, departments or contractors involved.
  5. Rerank and trim to what fits, keeping every item's source.

The summaries are the part often called graph-based retrieval: they let a question like "what is going wrong with drain works in the eastern suburbs" be answered from a few vetted paragraphs and then drilled into, instead of from hundreds of raw passages. They are written by the audit desk, reviewed like any other output, and stored as nodes with their own provenance and date.

docs.title: 4. Citations are enforced, not requested
docs.text:
• Every tool result carries fact ids. The answer must cite them.
  • After the agent composes an answer, a deterministic checker extracts each amount, date, identifier and proper name and confirms it occurs in a cited fact. A failure sends the answer back once with the unmatched items listed; a second failure returns a plain "the records we hold do not show this" with the nearest facts.
  • Every answer ends with what was not found and which office or request could supply it.
  • Each fact shows its tier and its date. A fact older than its source's normal refresh period shows a staleness mark.

docs.title: 5. Access tiers
docs.text:
Tier Who Sees Public Anyone Official and reviewed facts; residents' reports in aggregate; published briefs Contributor Signed-in residents Their own reports and subscriptions Researcher Registered journalists, academics, auditors Contractor network views, unreviewed flags marked as such, bulk queries Official Ward and department staff Their unit's work lists, pending items, correction requests Reviewer The platform's editors and lawyers Review queues, held items, everything above

Access is enforced in the query layer, by tier labels on nodes and relationships, so an agent acting for a public user cannot retrieve researcher-tier data however it is asked. Every query is logged with the tier it ran under.

docs.title: 6. What "enterprise grade" means here
docs.text: Property How it is met Correctness Quote check at load; citation check at answer; evaluation set run on every change Traceability Each fact records document, page, quote, extractor and version; each answer records the facts used Freshness Each source has an expected refresh period; a monitor flags sources that are late Availability Read paths use replicas and caches; the archive and graph are backed up; the public site degrades to cached pages Security Tiered access in the query layer; no secrets in agent sandboxes; residents' images stripped of faces and plates Privacy No private individuals' names stored; officials by post; deletion on request for contributors Multilingual Glossary, transliteration and a tested multilingual embedding model; answers in the asker's language Auditability Query and release logs; corrections recorded with reason and approver Cost control Routing keeps most questions off the expensive path; caching of views and summaries; budgets on agent sessions

docs.title: 7. Evaluation
docs.text:
Three sets, kept in the repository and run before any change to prompts, rules, ontology or retrieval goes live.

Set Size to start Measures Extraction 50 hand-labelled documents across types and both languages Field accuracy; share of quotes that match Questions 150 questions with verified answers, a third each in Marathi, Hindi and English, across all five routes Correct, cited, and "not known" said when true Refusals 40 questions the platform must not answer as asked (accusations, personal data, legal advice) Declines appropriately and offers what it can

Report results by route and by language. A change that improves English and worsens Marathi is not an improvement.

docs.title: Intelligence layer
docs.text:
Claude models do the reading, judging and writing. Managed Agents runs them as standing desks. LangGraph decides the order of work and where people must sign off. Plain code does everything that must be exact.

The first four desks and the pipeline already exist as files in ../mumbai-civic-graph/managed-agents/. This document extends them to the whole platform. Nothing here has been run against the API.

docs.title: 1. Division of labour
docs.text: Layer Decides Never does Plain code Quote checks, schema validation, graph writes, metric values, jurisdiction cards, citation checks, access control Interpret language LangGraph Which step runs next, fan-out, retries, pauses for people, saved state Reason about content Managed Agents How to split and carry out an agentic task inside one step Write to the graph or publish People Whether rules, merges, findings and briefs are released Bulk reading

docs.title: 2. Models
docs.text:
Use Model Why Desk leads; citizen answers; legal reading Claude Opus 5.5 Planning, judgement, accuracy Bulk document reading Claude Haiku 5.5 Most tokens are here; the task is narrow Verification, entity resolution, challenge, drafting Claude Sonnet 5.5 More judgement than reading, less than leading Question routing and entity spotting Claude Haiku 5.5 through the Messages API A single fast call, no agent needed

Overnight extraction of large backlogs can go through the Message Batches API at lower cost, since nothing is waiting on it. Model choices should be revisited against the evaluation sets; they are a starting allocation, not a measured optimum.

docs.title: 3. The desks
docs.text:
Six desks. Each is a Managed Agents coordinator with a small roster, except the Citizen desk, which is a single agent by design.

Desk Lead and roster Input Output Exists as files Intake Ingest lead; document extractor, fact verifier, entity resolver Archived documents Verified facts file, review file Yes Regulation Regulation lead; rule drafter, two equal-brief advocates Legal texts, directions, letters, orders Clauses, positions, candidate rules, dual-reading brief Planned Audit Audit lead; challenger, drafter The graph, for one ward or theme Brief, case files, drafts, gaps Yes Steward Steward lead; copies of itself The graph and the review queues Data-quality report: duplicates, orphans, stale sources, failed quote checks, schema drift; proposed fixes for a reviewer Planned Analyst Analyst lead; copies of itself for sub-questions A researcher's question A sourced research note Planned Citizen One agent One resident's question A sourced answer and a drafted letter Yes

Why the Steward desk matters: a civic graph decays. Portals change format, a contractor's name gains a suffix, a ward is split. One desk whose only job is to look for decay, and to propose rather than make corrections, is what keeps year two as trustworthy as week one.

Dynamic workflows are on for the Intake, Audit, Regulation and Analyst leads, so a large job runs as many agents in phases in the background. Every agent in a run uses tokens, so every session has a budget. To turn them off for a lead, set workflows: {type: disabled} in its file and apply again. The Citizen desk has no delegation at all.

docs.title: 4. Tools
docs.text:
For the hackathon, graph tools are custom tools answered by the client on a laptop. For the service, the same tools are hosted as an MCP server in front of the query layer, with credentials in a vault, so sessions run unattended.

Tool Returns Used by find_entity Nodes by name in any of three languages All locate Asset, ward, owning agency at a point Citizen, Audit trace_money Budget head to payment chain for a work or asset Citizen, Audit, Analyst who_is_responsible Agency, post, escalation, representative, contractor under liability Citizen which_authority Jurisdiction card for a plot or scheme Citizen, Regulation metric A metric's value with grain, sources and caveats Audit, Analyst, Citizen search Passages and summaries with fact ids, by the retrieval path in the search layer Analyst, Audit cypher_read Rows from one read-only query, tier-limited Audit, Analyst, Steward get_source Document reference and quote for a fact All gaps_for Missing records for a node, with the holder Audit, Citizen

No agent has a write tool. Outputs are files; code validates and loads them.

docs.title: 5. Memory
docs.text:
Store Holds Who writes Playbook Numbering conventions, abbreviations, extraction rules Intake and Steward leads; reviewed Ward notes Aliases, non-BMC roads, confirmed corrections, per ward Intake and Audit leads Legal notes How each regulation and direction has been read so far, with dates Regulation lead Source notes Each portal's quirks and format changes Steward lead

The Citizen desk mounts these read-only. Memory is versioned, so a wrong note can be traced and rolled back. No secrets and no personal data go into memory.

docs.title: 6. Workflows
docs.text:
Each is a LangGraph state graph with saved state. Steps in capitals pause for a person. The first exists as code; the rest follow the same pattern.

# Workflow Steps W1 Ingest and audit (exists) intake → quote check and load → REVIEW FACTS if many held → audit each ward in parallel → RELEASE → publish W2 Source watch for each source on its schedule: fetch or receive → detect new or changed documents → archive → hand to W1 or W4 → update freshness W3 Resident request route question → citizen desk → citation check → reply; if it is a report: locate → attach to asset → acknowledge → offer complaint draft W4 Legal change classify → regulation desk extracts clauses and positions → draft rules → LAWYER APPROVES RULES → recompute cards in code → notify affected subscribers → brief → RELEASE W5 RTI loop gap identified → drafter writes application → resident files and records the number → clock starts → at thirty days: draft first appeal → reply uploaded → intake → gap closed → audit re-run for affected ward W6 Correction and right of reply request received → steward desk checks against sources → REVIEWER DECIDES → correct with history kept, or attach the party's reply → notify requester W7 Stewardship weekly: steward desk scans → proposals queued → REVIEWER APPROVES MERGES AND FIXES → apply in code W8 Promotion gate any change to an agent, prompt, rule, ontology or retrieval → run the three evaluation sets → compare with the last release → OWNER APPROVES → apply new version

W2 and the scheduled parts of W1, W5 and W7 run as Managed Agents scheduled deployments once the graph tools are hosted. Each firing starts a fresh session; the LangGraph state carries what must persist between firings.

W8 is what makes changes safe. Agents are versioned, stored configurations, so a regression can be rolled back by pinning the previous version, and every fact records the version that extracted it.

docs.title: 7. Safeguards
docs.text: Risk Control Instructions hidden in documents or residents' messages Readers have no web, graph or publishing tools; outputs are validated in code; the citizen desk treats messages as requests, not rule changes Wrong fact Second reader; quote check at load; held queue; corrections workflow Wrong answer Tool-only answering; citation check in code; "not known" as a first-class reply Defamation Records, not verdicts; challenger on every finding; banned conclusion words in rubrics; officials by post; human release Bias toward one authority or party Equal-brief advocates; identical measures for all; published method; right of reply Privacy No private individuals; images blurred; contributor data deletable Runaway cost Session budgets; cheap models for bulk; routing keeps most questions off agents with delegation Model or platform change Evaluation gate; pinned agent versions; all prompts and rules in version control Over-reliance Every answer names its sources and gaps; the platform says it is not legal advice and not an official record

docs.title: 8. What a resident's question costs, in steps
docs.text:
To show that the common case is simple: "Who is responsible for the potholes on this road?"

  1. One fast call routes it as a trail question and finds the road.
  2. The citizen desk calls locate, who_is_responsible and trace_money: three graph queries.
  3. It writes a short answer and a complaint draft.
  4. Code checks the citations.

No delegation, no workflow run, no open-ended retrieval. The multi-agent machinery is for building and maintaining the graph, not for answering from it.

docs.title: Implementation plan
docs.text: Dates assume the event on 21 November 2026. Durations after that are planning estimates, not commitments, and depend most on how quickly data can be obtained.

docs.title: Phase 0: before the event (16 to 20 November)
docs.text:
Goal Tasks Know what data is real Open every P0 source in the catalogue; record format and access. Open five BMC road tenders on Mahatenders and note what detail, status and award pages show. Choose the stores Run HydraDB and Neo4j side by side with the competency queries; decide. Stand up Postgres with full-text, vector and spatial extensions. Have a spine Ward boundaries, named roads, corporators and the ward office's posts for one ward. Have a corpus Fifty tenders with notices and any awards; the roads budget pages for five years; two budget speeches. Archived with hashes. Have agents API key in hand; ant apply; one clean intake batch; rubrics tuned on real output. Have a yardstick Ten labelled documents and thirty verified questions.

Detail: ../mumbai-civic-graph/06-prep-and-day-plan.md.

docs.title: Phase 1: the day (21 November)
docs.text:
One ward. Graphs: Place, Money, Procurement, Works and Assets, Organisation and Jurisdiction, Evidence. Three applications on them.

Application Shows Work Coming to Your Street The platform is useful to a resident today Money trail with "who is responsible" The joins work: budget to tender to contractor to road to office Ward brief with one challenged case file and the gaps list The intelligence layer, and honesty about what is missing

Success on the day is a judge from the ward testing a road they know and getting a correct, sourced answer.

docs.title: 2. Build order within the platform
docs.text:
Each row depends on those above it.

  1. Archive and document registry
  2. Place spine and glossary
  3. Ontology core, shapes and the generated record schema
  4. Intake desk, quote check, loader
  5. Money and Procurement graphs
  6. Works and Assets; Organisation and Jurisdiction
  7. Named views and graph tools; Citizen desk
  8. Audit desk; challenger; release step
  9. Text, vector and spatial indexes; routing; citation checker
  10. Metrics engine
  11. Remaining graphs, one source at a time
  12. Hosted tools, schedules, public API

docs.title: 3. Team
docs.text:
Role Day Later Product and domain lead Decides scope; checks facts against reality Owns the roadmap and partnerships Data engineer Corpus, parsing, archive Source watch, pipelines Graph and ontology engineer Ontology, loader, queries Ontology governance, linked data AI engineer Agent files, rubrics, runs Evaluation, promotion gate, cost Search engineer Not needed on the day Indexes, routing, citation checker Front end Map, trail, chat Applications, review screen Lawyer Wording review Rules approval, right of reply, publication sign-off Editor or journalist Finds the story Release decisions, newsroom feed Community organiser Ground truth in the ward Residents' groups, voice access, pilots Marathi and Hindi reviewer Checks every public sentence Glossary, evaluation in both languages

Four or five people cover the day by doubling up. The lawyer and the language reviewer are the two roles that cannot be skipped once anything is public.

docs.title: 4. Infrastructure
docs.text:
Component Day Service Graph One container on a laptop HydraDB on object storage, or Neo4j, with backups Relational, spatial, text, vector One Postgres container Managed Postgres; OpenSearch if volume requires Archive A folder with a manifest S3-compatible bucket with versioning Agents Managed Agents, sessions started from a laptop Managed Agents with hosted tools and scheduled deployments Orchestration LangGraph with a SQLite checkpoint file LangGraph with a Postgres checkpointer Application and API A local web server A small container service behind a content delivery network Observability Console session traces Tracing, cost and freshness dashboards, alerts

Running costs are driven by three things: tokens for bulk extraction (one-off per document, lowest on the smallest model and in batches), tokens for audits and briefs (bounded by session budgets and schedule), and tokens for residents' questions (kept low by routing). Measure each in the first month before forecasting; this plan does not estimate them.

docs.title: 5. Governance
docs.text: Matter Rule Ownership A neutral host: a university centre or an established civic organisation, not a vendor and not a party Editorial A small board including a lawyer and a journalist approves anything naming a party; decisions are logged Method Ontology, rules, rubrics and metric definitions are public Corrections Anyone can request one; each is answered; history is kept Right of reply Any named party's response is published beside the record Data licence Open licence for official-tier data; residents' contributions under clear consent Privacy Compliance with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act; no private individuals; deletion on request Independence No funding from contractors or developers with civic contracts; funders listed publicly Relationship with BMC Offered as a partner tool; the platform never presents itself as an official record

docs.title: 6. Adoption path
docs.text:
1. A ward office. The liability watch and the complaint routing reduce their load. Ask for nothing but a meeting and feedback.
  2. Corporators and residents' associations. Ward briefs and meeting questions; fund tracking for those who volunteer.
  3. Newsrooms. The weekly feed, on equal terms.
  4. BMC's IT and finance departments. The Open Publishing Kit: data published at source replaces reading PDFs after the fact.
  5. The state Urban Development Department. The shared redevelopment register for disputes between authorities.

Each step produces evidence of use that makes the next conversation easier.

docs.title: 7. Measures
docs.text: Area Measure Coverage Share of wards, departments and years in each graph; share of capital budget traced to at least a tender Quality Extraction accuracy; quote-match rate; evaluation scores by route and language; corrections per thousand facts Freshness Share of sources updated within their expected period Use Residents asking; subscriptions; complaints and RTIs drafted and filed; newsroom stories citing the platform Effect Defects repaired under liability; RTI gaps closed; audit observations answered; promises with evidence Trust Corrections resolved; replies published; officials using the work lists

docs.title: 8. Risks
docs.text: Risk Mitigation Data cannot be obtained at the pace planned Start where data is open; show gaps and file RTIs; partner for the rest; cut scope, never quality Portals change or block collection Source watch detects it; fall back to requests and assisted collection; never defeat access controls A wrong fact about a named party is published The layered checks above; fast, visible correction; legal review before release Seen as partisan Identical treatment, public method, mixed editorial board HydraDB proves immature Bolt-only access and a tested Neo4j fallback Dependence on one model provider or beta features Prompts, rules and evaluations in version control; agents behind a thin client; the graph and archive are independent of any model Cost grows with use Routing, caching, budgets, batches; measure before scaling Team disperses after the event Open everything; find the host organisation early; keep the first slice small enough for two people to run Marathi quality lags English A named reviewer; evaluation reported by language; no release that regresses either

docs.title: 9. The first ten things to do
docs.text:
1. Get an API key working and run the dry-run pipeline, then one real intake batch.
  2. Open five BMC road tenders on Mahatenders and write down exactly what each page shows.
  3. Choose the ward.
  4. Run both graph databases against the ten competency questions.
  5. Download the roads budget pages for five years and check that leaf totals reconcile.
  6. Build the place spine for the ward.
  7. Hand-label ten documents and write thirty questions.
  8. Ask the organisers what data the authorities will bring.
  9. Recruit a lawyer and a Marathi reviewer.
  10. Write the three-minute demo script, then cut everything not needed for it.

docs.title: User personas
docs.text:
Who Aamcha Hishob serves, what each of them is trying to get done, and which parts of the platform do it for them.

These personas are composites drawn from the challenge brief and the kinds of people it invites. They are not research. Before building, test each one with two or three real people who fit it, and rewrite what does not hold.

docs.title: 1. Summary
docs.text:
# Persona Group Main question Channel Tier 1 Sunita, resident of a chawl Residents "Who will fix this, and how do I make them?" WhatsApp voice note, Marathi Public 2 Imran, salaried commuter Residents "When will this road work end?" Web on phone, alerts Contributor 3 Lata, housing society secretary Residents "What is planned for our lane, and is our building on any list?" Web, WhatsApp Contributor 4 Ramesh, family awaiting a transit home Residents "When do we get our home, and who is holding it up?" WhatsApp, community worker Public 5 Farah, residents' association volunteer Organisers "What do we ask at the ward meeting, with proof?" Web, printed briefs Contributor 6 Kavita, RTI activist Organisers "Which record is missing, and how do I get it?" Web Contributor 7 Arjun, civic reporter at a Marathi daily Watchdogs "What is the story this week, and can I stand behind it?" Weekly feed, web Researcher 8 Dr Meera, urban policy researcher Watchdogs "Can I query the whole thing and cite it?" API, bulk downloads Researcher 9 Corporator Pawar Representatives "What is happening in my ward that I should raise?" Web, ward brief Official 10 Assistant Engineer, ward office Officials "Which defects can the contractor be made to fix, and which complaints are mine?" Web work list Official 11 Deputy Secretary, state Urban Development Department Officials "What do both authorities' records actually show?" Briefs, register Official 12 Advocate Nair, the platform's reviewing lawyer Platform team "Is this safe and fair to publish?" Review screen Reviewer

Two further groups use the platform without being its audience: contractors and developers, who appear in the records and need a way to correct them and reply; and other builders, who use the public API. Both are covered in section 4.

docs.title: 2.1 Sunita, 46, resident of a chawl in a dense ward
docs.text:
Situation. Lives with her family in one room. Reads Marathi slowly, does not use English. Uses WhatsApp daily, mostly by voice. Her lane's drain overflows every monsoon and the open manhole near the tap has been reported twice.

Jobs to be done. - Find out who is responsible for the drain and the manhole. - Send a complaint that is not ignored, and know when to push again.

Pains today. Complaints are closed without the work being done. She is sent between offices. She does not know the names of departments or posts.

What she needs from the platform. - Send a voice note and a photo; get a short spoken or written reply in Marathi. - Be asked where it is if the location is missing, and have the place read back to her. - A complaint she can forward or have printed, addressed to the right office. - A reminder when the complaint's time limit passes, with the next step.

Features. Voice line (idea 37), Jawabdar (idea 2), Complaint Closure Audit (idea 31), citizen desk.

Design notes. No sign-in. Short replies. No jargon or abbreviations. Never ask her for more than one thing at a time. Faces and number plates removed from her photos; her phone number never stored with her report.

Success looks like. The manhole is covered, and she knows which office to call next time.

docs.title: 2.2 Imran, 31, salaried commuter
docs.text:
Situation. Rents a flat in the western suburbs. Comfortable with apps in English and Hindi. His road has been dug up for months.

Jobs to be done. - Know what is being built on his route, by whom, and by when. - Know when a deadline has passed.

Features. Work Coming to Your Street (idea 14), Site Board QR (idea 15), Paisa Trail (idea 1), Pothole Ledger (idea 18).

Design notes. Save a route or an area once; alerts arrive without asking. Every alert shows the tender number and a link to the source.

Success looks like. He can say, with the tender in hand, that the work is three months late, and to whom.

docs.title: 2.3 Lata, 58, secretary of a cooperative housing society
docs.text:
Situation. Handles the society's dealings with the ward office. The building is old. Redevelopment is being discussed.

Jobs to be done. - Know whether the building is on the dangerous-buildings list, and what that requires. - Know what is planned for the lane and the nearby reserved plot. - If redevelopment proceeds, know which authority has the file and at what stage.

Features. Safety List (idea 19), Reserved Plots Tracker (idea 22), Ek Plot Ek Record (idea 41), ward budget summary (idea 7).

Design notes. Pages she can print for a society meeting. Plain statements of what is official and what is not. Clear "this is not legal advice" wording on anything about approvals.

Success looks like. The society's meeting decides with the same facts in front of everyone.

docs.title: 2.4 Ramesh, 52, head of a family displaced by a road project
docs.text:
Situation. Moved out for a project, promised a permanent transit home. Rent was paid for a while, then stopped. Does not know which scheme his home is supposed to come from.

Jobs to be done. - Know which schemes owe transit homes near him, and how many have been handed over. - Know whom to approach, and with what.

Features. Tenement Ledger and resident's front door in Ek Plot Ek Record (idea 41), Stalled Rehab Tracker (idea 28), drafted letters.

Design notes. Reached most often through a community worker or housing rights group, so the platform must work well when someone else is operating it for him. Records are counts per scheme; the platform never holds allotment lists or names.

Success looks like. He knows the scheme, its due date and the office, and his group can raise it with numbers.

docs.title: 2.5 Farah, 39, residents' association volunteer
docs.text:
Situation. Organises a residents' group in her ward. Attends ward committee meetings. Writes letters on behalf of neighbours.

Jobs to be done. - Arrive at a meeting with a few questions that cannot be brushed aside. - Track what was promised for the ward, and whether it started. - Collect neighbours' reports into evidence.

Features. Ward brief and meeting questions (audit desk), Vachan Tracker (idea 3), Unspent Money Watch (idea 6), Committee Digest (idea 29), Complaint Closure Audit (idea 31).

Design notes. One-page outputs, each fact with its source in brackets. A way to share a page as an image on WhatsApp groups.

Success looks like. A question she asks gets a dated answer in the minutes.

docs.title: 2.6 Kavita, 44, RTI activist
docs.text:
Situation. Files dozens of right-to-information requests a year. Holds boxes of replies. Spends much of her time drafting and appealing.

Jobs to be done. - Ask for exactly the record that fills a gap. - Track the thirty-day clock and file appeals on time. - Make replies useful beyond one person.

Features. RTI Commons (idea 30), the gaps list from the audit desk, RTI loop workflow (W5), intake of replies.

Design notes. Applications drafted to ask for named records by period; appeal drafts ready on day thirty-one. Her name and address removed from any reply she shares.

Success looks like. Her replies close gaps in the graph and are reused by others.

docs.title: 2.7 Arjun, 29, civic reporter at a Marathi daily
docs.text:
Situation. Covers the corporation alone. Short of time. Cannot run a story on a hunch.

Jobs to be done. - Find the week's story in the committee agenda, tender awards and audit reports. - Check a claim fast, with the document behind it.

Features. Newsroom Feed (idea 38), Committee Digest (idea 29), Audit Para Tracker (idea 32), Mega Project Meter (idea 11), contractor record (idea 4, researcher tier).

Design notes. Every item carries its documents and the Challenger's counter-argument, so the other side's response is anticipated. The same feed goes to every outlet on the same terms. Clear marking of official record versus residents' report.

Success looks like. A published story that cites the platform and survives the corporation's reply.

docs.title: 2.8 Dr Meera, 41, urban policy researcher
docs.text:
Situation. Studies municipal finance and planning. Comfortable with data tools.

Jobs to be done. - Query across years, wards and departments. - Cite data with its provenance in published work.

Features. Public Data Service and API (idea 40), bulk exports in JSON lines, Parquet and Turtle, analyst desk, metric definitions.

Design notes. Stable identifiers, documented ontology, release versions she can cite, and a statement of coverage and gaps with each release.

Success looks like. Her paper's numbers can be reproduced from a named release.

docs.title: 2.9 Corporator Pawar, elected representative
docs.text:
Situation. Represents an electoral ward. Hears residents' complaints daily. Has a discretionary fund.

Jobs to be done. - Know what is late or stuck in the ward before residents tell him. - Raise questions in committee with evidence. - Show residents what his fund paid for.

Features. Ward brief, Corporator Fund Tracker (idea 8), Corporator Report Card (idea 34), Ward Participatory Budget (idea 36).

Design notes. Identical measures for every corporator, regardless of party. A route to publish his own fund records. A right to correct his record.

Success looks like. He uses the brief in committee, and volunteers his fund data.

docs.title: 2.10 Assistant Engineer (Roads), ward office
docs.text:
Situation. Responsible for roads in one ward. Many complaints, some about roads that are not the corporation's. Contractors on recently built roads owe repairs under their defect liability periods.

Jobs to be done. - See which complaints are genuinely his and which belong to another agency. - See which defects are on roads still under contractor liability, grouped by contractor. - Correct the record where it is wrong.

Features. Liability watch (audit desk), Pothole Ledger (idea 18), complaint routing in Jawabdar (idea 2), correction workflow (W6).

Design notes. Addressed by post, never by name. A work list, not a scorecard. A correction button that is answered.

Success looks like. Repairs done at the contractor's cost that would otherwise have been paid from the ward's budget. This persona is the platform's best route to adoption.

docs.title: 2.11 Deputy Secretary, state Urban Development Department
docs.text:
Situation. Fields letters from both BMC and SRA on the same regulation. Needs to decide on evidence, not on correspondence.

Jobs to be done. - See every scheme in question, both authorities' actions on it, and delivery against the regulation's purpose. - Read both positions set out fairly, with the texts each relies on.

Features. Ek Plot Ek Record (idea 41): Scheme Register, Tenement Ledger, Concession Meter, dual-reading brief.

Design notes. Neutral language, equal treatment, every claim sourced. Both authorities invited to correct their own records before anything is public.

Success looks like. The next direction cites figures from the register.

docs.title: 2.12 Advocate Nair, reviewing lawyer for the platform
docs.text:
Situation. Volunteers part of her week. Signs off anything that names a party.

Jobs to be done. - Review findings, rules and briefs quickly, with the evidence and the challenge alongside. - Hold anything unsafe or unfair.

Features. Review screen at the release and rule-approval steps of the LangGraph workflows; Challenger reviews; correction and right-of-reply workflow.

Design notes. Each item shows the claim, the evidence table, the Challenger's review and the banned-word check. One-click hold with a reason that goes back to the audit desk.

Success looks like. Nothing published needs to be withdrawn.

docs.title: 4. People who appear in the records
docs.text: Group Need How the platform meets it Contractors and developers Accuracy; a right to respond Records shown as stages and dates, not verdicts; correction requests answered; replies published beside the record Officials Not to be singled out personally Named by post only; work lists rather than rankings Elected representatives Equal treatment Identical measures for all; right to correct BMC, SRA and other agencies Fair representation Invited to correct their own records before release; positions set out in their own words

docs.title: 5. Anti-personas
docs.text:
The platform is deliberately not built for these uses.

Use Why not, and what happens instead Someone seeking to target an individual official or resident No private individuals in the data; officials by post; harassment-shaped requests declined A campaign wanting one-sided material against a party or authority Same rules and measures for all; counter-arguments shown with every finding Someone wanting legal advice on their own case Plain statement that the platform summarises published records; pointed to the right office or to legal aid Someone wanting an official certificate or record The platform is not an official record; pointed to the issuing office

docs.title: 6. Priorities for the first slice
docs.text:
For the hackathon day and the first 30 days, design for three personas first and let the others follow:

  1. Sunita, because if it works for her by voice in Marathi it works for nearly everyone.
  2. Farah, because she turns the platform's output into action in a room where decisions are made.
  3. The Assistant Engineer, because an officer who gains from it is how the city adopts it.

Arjun is the fourth: one published story reaches more residents than any feature.

docs.title: 7. Validating the personas
docs.text: Step How Interview Two or three people per persona before the 30-day mark; ask what they did the last time they had this problem Test the first slice Watch Sunita-type and Farah-type users complete one task each, in their language, without help Measure Task completed, time taken, whether the answer was correct, whether they would use it again Update Rewrite this file from what is learned; record what changed and why

docs.title: What has and has not been verified
docs.text:
These records were written on 15 November 2026 without an AWS account to test in. Service facts come from AWS pages found by search and from general knowledge; each record lists what to confirm. In particular:

  • Confirmed by AWS pages found in search: Neptune's openCypher endpoint works over Bolt and HTTPS; Neptune Analytics supports vector search; S3 Vectors is generally available; AWS End User Messaging Social has an endpoint in Mumbai; Amazon Transcribe lists Marathi for batch transcription.
  • Not confirmed: Neptune Serverless's minimum capacity and whether it can pause; Aurora Serverless v2 pausing to zero in Mumbai; whether Textract reads Devanagari; whether Claude Platform on AWS is offered from the Mumbai region; any price.
  • From Anthropic's documentation as bundled with this tool: Claude Platform on AWS has the same API as Anthropic's own, including Managed Agents in beta; Amazon Bedrock does not offer Managed Agents.

No prices are quoted. Price each option in the AWS calculator for Mumbai before committing.

docs.title: Design and architecture
docs.text: Aamcha Hishob on AWS. Read with the platform documents one level up; this file covers how it is built and run, and points to the decision record behind each choice.

docs.title: 1. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
A public service that answers, with sources, questions about how Mumbai's civic bodies allocate money, award contracts, carry out works and assign responsibility. It ingests published documents and residents' contributions, builds a knowledge graph, and serves residents, reporters, officials and other builders.

Out of scope: acting as an official record; filing complaints into government systems automatically; storing data about private individuals.

docs.title: 2. Requirements that shape the design
docs.text:
Quality Requirement Design response Correctness No fact without a source; no answer without citations Quote check at load, citation check at answer, both in code Rebuildability Any store can be lost and rebuilt Archive and facts ledger on S3 are the record (ADR 0001) Low fixed cost A civic project with little money must survive quiet months Serverless and scale-down choices; two profiles (ADR 0021) Small team Two people must be able to run it Managed services over self-run clusters; no Kubernetes (ADR 0012) Portability No single vendor can end the project Open formats on S3, Bolt for the graph, Postgres, prompts and rules in git Safety Untrusted documents and messages must not steer the system Agents have no write or publish tools; graph is private (ADR 0011) Languages Marathi, Hindi and English as equals Glossary, tested embedding model, evaluation by language Accountability of the platform itself Every release and correction is traceable Run, release and correction records; versioned agents

Planning assumptions, to replace with measurements: tens of thousands of documents in the first year; a graph of a few million nodes and edges; residents' questions in the low thousands per day at most; intake in batches, not real time.
