                                    │                          (Messages, Batches,   │
                                    │                           Managed Agents)      │
                                    └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        Cognito (sign-in, tiers) · Secrets Manager · KMS · CloudWatch · OpenTelemetry
Component Role Record S3 archive Every source document, immutable, with hash and fetch metadata 0001 S3 facts ledger Validated facts as append-only files, the input to every projection 0001 Graph database The ten graphs, for traversal 0004 Aurora PostgreSQL Geometry, text and vector search, workflow state, review queues, metrics, accounts 0006, 0007 worker service Runs LangGraph workflows, starts agent sessions, answers their graph tool calls 0010, 0011 loader service Schema validation, quote check, writes to graph and indexes 0001 api service Query layer: routing, named views, metrics, access tiers, citation check 0014 public-mcp service The same read-only tools for outside assistants and builders 0011 Claude Platform on AWS Models, batches and Managed Agents 0002, 0003 Queues and scheduler Triggers and back-pressure 0013 Static site and tiles Web application and maps 0015 WhatsApp and speech Resident channels 0016

docs.title: 5.1 Ingest
docs.text:
source ─► fetch or upload ─► S3 archive (hash, metadata) ─► S3 event ─► queue
      ─► worker: parse (text layer, else vision) ─► S3 parsed text
      ─► worker: W1 workflow ─► Managed Agents intake session
                                 (documents mounted as files; no network)
      ─► session outputs: facts, review, report ─► S3 staging
      ─► loader: schema check ─► quote check against parsed page ─► held queue or
         S3 facts ledger (append) ─► graph upsert ─► text and vector index ─► metrics refresh

The facts ledger is the hinge. Everything before it is extraction and can be redone with a better prompt; everything after it is projection and can be rebuilt with a different engine.

docs.title: 5.2 Answer
docs.text:
question ─► api: normalise, glossary, entities (one fast model call)
         ─► route: lookup · trail · metric · rule · exploratory
         ─► named view / metric engine / rules engine / hybrid retrieval, tier-filtered
         ─► citizen desk composes from tool results (Managed Agents session via worker)
         ─► api: citation check in code ─► reply with sources, tier, gaps

Lookups, trails, metrics and rule cards can also be served with no agent at all, as plain pages. The agent is used when the resident asks in free language or wants a letter drafted.

docs.title: 5.3 Audit and release
docs.text:
schedule ─► queue ─► worker: W1 from the audit step, one branch per ward
         ─► audit session (lead, challenger, drafter) ─► outputs to S3 staging
         ─► workflow pauses ─► reviewer decides in the review screen
         ─► approved outputs copied to public S3 prefix ─► site and feeds update

docs.title: 6. Storage layout
docs.text:
s3://nagar-archive/      source/<publisher>/<yyyy>/<sha256>.<ext>   + .meta.json     (versioned, object lock)
s3://nagar-data/         parsed/<sha256>/page-<n>.txt
                         facts/<graph>/<yyyy-mm-dd>/<batch>.jsonl                   (append-only)
                         staging/<session>/…                                         (expires)
                         exports/<release>/{jsonl,parquet,ttl}/…
s3://nagar-public/       site/ · tiles/ · published/<ward>/ · downloads/

Postgres schemas: geo (wards, roads, plots), search (passages, vectors, summaries), flow (LangGraph checkpoints, queues, reviews), metric (computed values), account (users, tiers, subscriptions), registry (documents, sources, freshness, runs).

docs.title: 7. Network and security
docs.text:
• One VPC in Mumbai across two availability zones. Databases and services sit in private subnets. Only CloudFront and the load balancer face the internet.
  • The graph database has no public address. Agents never connect to it; they call tools that the worker answers (ADR 0011).
  • Managed Agents sandboxes run on Anthropic's side with no outbound hosts allowed and the web tools off. Documents reach them as mounted files; results leave as output files.
  • Outbound calls to Claude go through a NAT gateway or a private endpoint if one is offered. Requests are signed with the task's IAM role; there is no long-lived API key.
  • Each service has its own task role with the least access it needs: the loader can write the graph, the api can only read, the worker can start sessions and read and write staging.
  • Encryption with KMS at rest; TLS in transit. Secrets in Secrets Manager.
  • WAF rate limits and bot rules in front of the api and the public tools.
  • Residents' images are stripped of faces and number plates, and messages of phone numbers, before storage or any model call (ADR 0018).

docs.title: 8. Deployment profiles
docs.text:
Lean (pilot, lowest fixed cost) Standard (public service) Graph Neo4j Community, one Graviton instance, volume snapshots Neptune Database Serverless, two zones Postgres Aurora Serverless v2, lowest setting, pausing if available Aurora Serverless v2 with a reader Search Inside Postgres Postgres, or OpenSearch Service if measurements call for it Services One task each on Fargate Spot where safe Two tasks each across zones, autoscaling Networking One NAT instance or gateway NAT gateways per zone, VPC endpoints Environments One account, two stages Three accounts: development, staging, production Recovery Rebuild from S3 Rebuild from S3, plus database snapshots for speed

Both profiles use the same code and the same S3 record. Moving from lean to standard is a rebuild of projections, not a migration of truth.

docs.title: A resident asks on WhatsApp
docs.text:
1. WhatsApp message arrives through End User Messaging and lands on a queue.
  2. The worker redacts personal details, transcribes a voice note if there is one, and passes the text to the api.
  3. The api routes the question. For a trail, it runs named views directly.
  4. If free-language composition is needed, the worker opens a citizen desk session, answers its tool calls from the api, and collects the reply.
  5. The api checks citations and returns the answer; the worker sends it to WhatsApp.

docs.title: A new state direction is published
docs.text:
1. Source watch archives the document and classifies it as legal text.
  2. The legal-change workflow starts a Regulation desk session; outputs are candidate rules with quotes.
  3. The workflow pauses. A lawyer approves or edits the rules in the review screen.
  4. Code recomputes jurisdiction cards, writes changed cards to the ledger, and notifies subscribers of affected plots.

docs.title: An agent definition changes
docs.text:
1. A pull request edits an agent file, rubric or rule.
  2. CI applies it to the staging workspace and runs the three evaluation sets.
  3. Results are compared with the last release by route and by language.
  4. An owner approves; the change is applied to production. The earlier agent version stays available for rollback.

docs.title: 10. Failure and degradation
docs.text: Failure Behaviour Claude service unavailable or rate limited Lookups, trails, metrics and cards still work as pages; free-language answers show a notice; intake queues wait Graph database down Site serves cached pages and published briefs from S3; api returns a clear notice; rebuild or failover A portal changes format Source watch flags the source as late; nothing wrong is loaded because the quote check fails closed A bad prompt change slips through Roll back to the pinned agent version; re-extract affected documents, identified by the version recorded on each fact Wrong fact published Correction workflow; history kept; affected answers identified through the facts they cited

docs.title: 11. Open items
docs.text:
1. Confirm Claude Platform on AWS can be used from an account whose workloads are in Mumbai, and what a session's six-hour unattended limit means for long intake runs.
  2. Run the ten competency queries on Neptune, Neo4j and HydraDB and record what each rejects.
  3. Price both profiles in Mumbai.
  4. Test two or three embedding models on a hundred real Marathi and Hindi questions.
  5. Test scanned Marathi committee papers through each parsing route.
  6. Ask a lawyer about cross-border processing of residents' messages under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.
  7. Decide the host organisation; it owns the AWS accounts.

docs.title: ADR 0001: The document archive and facts ledger on S3 are the system of record
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The platform holds the same knowledge in several stores: a graph, a text index, a vector index, metric tables. Any of them may need to be replaced as the project grows or as a product proves unsuitable. Extraction prompts will also improve, and old documents will need re-reading.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option For Against Graph database is the record One place to look Engine choice becomes irreversible; backups and migrations are critical; re-extraction means editing live data Relational database is the record, graph derived Mature tooling Still couples truth to one engine; awkward for document-shaped facts Immutable archive plus append-only facts files on S3; every store is a projection Any store can be rebuilt or swapped; cheap, durable; full history for free; re-extraction is a new batch A rebuild step is needed; consistency across projections is eventual

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Two S3 datasets are the record. The archive holds every source document unchanged, addressed by content hash, with versioning and object lock. The facts ledger holds validated facts as append-only JSON lines, partitioned by graph and date, each carrying source, page, quote, tier, extractor version and ontology version. The graph, the search indexes and the metric tables are built from the ledger by the loader and can be dropped and rebuilt.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The graph engine in ADR 0004 can change without data loss.
  • Corrections are new ledger entries that supersede old ones; nothing is edited in place.
  • A full rebuild must be scripted, timed and rehearsed (ADR 0022).
  • Readers may briefly see a projection that lags the ledger; the loader records the last batch applied to each store.

docs.title: Revisit when
docs.text: A rebuild takes longer than the service can tolerate being stale.

docs.title: ADR 0002: Reach Claude through Claude Platform on AWS
docs.text: Status: Accepted, subject to one confirmation · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The platform uses Claude models, the Message Batches API for overnight extraction, the Files API, and Managed Agents with multi-agent rosters, outcomes and memory stores. Hosting is on AWS, and the host organisation will want one bill and IAM-based access control.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option For Against Amazon Bedrock AWS-operated; familiar to AWS teams; own batch and guardrail features Per Anthropic's documentation it does not offer Managed Agents, the Message Batches API or the Files API; feature releases follow AWS's schedule; model ids carry a prefix Anthropic API direct Full feature set; simplest to start Separate billing and credentials; a long-lived API key to manage Claude Platform on AWS Operated by Anthropic with the same API as its own platform, including Managed Agents (beta), batches and files; SigV4 and IAM; billing through AWS Marketplace Newer offering; an unattended session must be re-authenticated after six hours; sessions on self-hosted sandboxes cannot attach memory stores

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Use Claude Platform on AWS. Services authenticate with their IAM task roles; no API key is stored. The client code selects the AWS client when ANTHROPIC_AWS_WORKSPACE_ID is set and the standard client otherwise, so a laptop with an ordinary key and a Fargate task with a role run the same code.

For the hackathon day, the Anthropic API with event credits is fine; nothing in the code changes.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Agent sessions must finish, or receive an event, within six hours. Intake batches are sized accordingly and long jobs are split by the workflow.
  • Cloud sandboxes are used so memory stores remain available (ADR 0003).
  • If the platform ever had to move to Bedrock, the agent layer would need rebuilding on a different runtime. The facts ledger, graph and search would be unaffected.

docs.title: To confirm
docs.text:
• That the offering can be subscribed to and called from an account whose workloads run in Mumbai, and which region the endpoint is in.
  • IAM actions needed by each service.

docs.title: ADR 0003: Run agents on Claude Managed Agents with cloud sandboxes
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Six desks of agents read documents, verify, audit, challenge and draft. They need a sandbox with a filesystem, delegation between agents, rubric-graded outcomes, persistent memory, and versioned configurations.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option For Against Claude Managed Agents, cloud sandboxes Anthropic runs the loop and the sandbox; rosters, background workflow runs, outcomes, memory stores, versioned agents and session budgets are built in; agent definitions already written Beta; sandbox runs outside our VPC; platform dependency Managed Agents with self-hosted sandboxes in our VPC Tools execute inside our network More to operate; on Claude Platform on AWS such sessions cannot attach memory stores Amazon Bedrock AgentCore AWS-native runtime, identity and memory A different agent model and API; the existing agent files, outcomes and roster design would not carry over; depends on Bedrock's Claude feature set Own agent loop on Fargate (Messages API with tools, or the Claude Agent SDK) Full control; no beta dependency We would build and maintain delegation, grading, memory, sandboxing and versioning ourselves LangGraph agents calling the Messages API One framework for everything Same build burden for sandbox and delegation; mixes deterministic orchestration with agentic work

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Managed Agents with cloud sandboxes. Sandboxes have no outbound hosts and the web tools are off. Documents enter as mounted files and results leave as output files. Agent, environment and memory definitions live as files in git and are applied with the ant CLI from CI.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The sandbox never needs to reach our network, which is what allows the graph to stay private (ADR 0011).
  • Only public documents and redacted text are mounted into sandboxes.
  • A fallback exists in principle (own loop on Fargate) but is not built. The agent prompts, rubrics and tool definitions are plain files and would carry over.

docs.title: Revisit when
docs.text: A requirement arises to process material that may not leave the VPC, or the beta terms change.

docs.title: ADR 0004: Graph database
docs.text: Status: Accepted for the two profiles; HydraDB on trial · 15 November 2026 Changes: the earlier plan named HydraDB as primary. For hosting on AWS this record makes it a trial candidate.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The graph serves multi-hop reads over a few million nodes and edges. Writes come only from the loader, in batches. Because of ADR 0001 the graph is a rebuildable projection, so durability features matter less than usual and operating effort and fixed cost matter more. All access goes through one repository layer over Bolt, using a common openCypher subset with no vendor procedures.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Model and query For Against Amazon Neptune Database, Serverless Property graph (openCypher, Gremlin) and RDF (SPARQL) Managed, multi-zone, IAM, backups; openCypher over Bolt works with standard drivers; scales with load A capacity floor that is paid when idle; openCypher is a subset without APOC; no built-in vector index; text search through a separate OpenSearch integration; property graph and RDF data are separate stores Amazon Neptune Analytics Property graph, openCypher, in memory Vector search and graph algorithms built in; pairs with Bedrock's graph retrieval Provisioned capacity; aimed at analysis, not as the serving store Neo4j Community, self-managed on one instance Property graph, full Cypher Richest Cypher; vector and full-text indexes; RDF import plugin; lowest fixed cost at small scale; identical to the laptop setup Single node, no clustering or online backup in the community edition; GPLv3; we patch and monitor it Neo4j Aura through AWS Marketplace As above, managed No operations Cost; data sits in the vendor's account HydraDB on S3 with stateless nodes on Fargate Property graph, openCypher subset, Bolt Object storage is the source of truth, which suits S3 and low idle cost; open core Version 0.3; few independent evaluations; Cypher coverage must be checked query by query; Elastic License 2.0; no text or vector index Memgraph, FalkorDB Property graph, Cypher, in memory Fast Source-available licences; memory-bound; self-managed Kuzu, embedded Property graph No server at all; could sit inside the api task Community-maintained; single writer; less suited to a shared service

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Standard profile: Neptune Database Serverless. A two-person team should not run a database cluster, and Bolt support keeps the code unchanged.
  • Lean profile and local development: Neo4j Community on one instance, rebuilt from the ledger if lost.
  • HydraDB: trial. Deploy beside the chosen engine, load from the same ledger, and run the competency queries and a soak test. Adopt it for the lean profile if it passes; its storage model is the best fit for a low-traffic public dataset on S3.
  • Neptune Analytics: not now. Add it later, loaded from the same ledger, if graph algorithms (community detection for the contractor graph) are needed at scale.

Vector and text search stay outside the graph in every case (ADR 0007), so the graph engines are compared on traversal alone.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Queries must stay within the subset all three engines accept. A test suite runs the named views against each.
  • Date arithmetic, MERGE behaviour and variable-length paths are the known places engines differ; the loader precomputes derived dates so queries compare plain values.
  • Community detection runs offline in Python and writes results back, whichever engine is used.

docs.title: To confirm
docs.text:
• Neptune Serverless's minimum capacity and whether it can pause when idle; price both profiles.
  • Which of the ten competency queries each engine rejects.

docs.title: Revisit when
docs.text: HydraDB passes its trial, or the Neptune floor proves too costly for the traffic.

docs.title: ADR 0005: Ontology in Turtle and SHACL, enforced in the pipeline; RDF published as files
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The platform needs a formal ontology for consistency and for others to reuse, and wants to publish linked open data. The serving store is a property graph.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option For Against RDF triple store as the primary store (Neptune SPARQL, Jena Fuseki, Oxigraph) Native ontology, reasoning and validation Path-heavy application queries are harder; fewer developers know SPARQL; two query languages in the application Both models live in Neptune One managed service Neptune keeps RDF and property graph data separately, so everything is loaded and kept in step twice Ontology and shapes as files; validation in the loader; property graph for serving; RDF generated as an export Ontology discipline without a reasoner in the serving path; one query language in the application; linked data still published No live inference; SPARQL users query dumps or a later endpoint

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The ontology (OWL in Turtle), SHACL shapes and SKOS glossary live in git. A build step generates the extraction record schema and the loader's whitelist from them. The loader validates each batch with pySHACL before it reaches the ledger. Each release exports the official-tier graph as Turtle to S3 for download.

A live SPARQL endpoint (Oxigraph on Fargate, loaded from the export) is added only when someone asks for one.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Anything that would be inferred is materialised by the loader as explicit facts marked derived.
  • Ontology changes go through the evaluation gate and bump a version recorded on every fact.

docs.title: ADR 0006: Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 for relational, spatial and operational data
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Besides the graph, the platform needs geometry (wards, roads, plots), workflow checkpoints, review queues, accounts and subscriptions, computed metrics, a document registry, and, at first, search (ADR 0007).

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option For Against Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 PostGIS, full-text and pgvector in one managed database; scales with load and, where supported, pauses when idle; multi-zone; LangGraph has a Postgres checkpointer Costs more per unit than plain RDS when busy; cold start after a pause RDS for PostgreSQL Simple, predictable price, same extensions Fixed instance size; no pause Postgres on an instance or in a container Cheapest We run backups, patching and failover DynamoDB for operational data, separate spatial store Truly serverless No spatial or text search; more moving parts; awkward for review queues and joins

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: One Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 cluster with PostGIS and pgvector, separate schemas per concern. The lean profile runs it at the lowest setting; the standard profile adds a reader.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One database to secure, back up and monitor.
  • Search and workflow state share a cluster at first; split them if either starves the other.

docs.title: To confirm
docs.text: Pausing to zero capacity and extension versions in Mumbai.

docs.title: ADR 0007: Hybrid search in Postgres first; OpenSearch when measurements call for it
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Search must find exact identifiers and names (tender numbers, road names in two scripts), answer everyday-language questions across three languages, filter by ward and by access tier, and return passages linked to graph nodes so retrieval can move into the graph. Most residents' questions never reach open-ended retrieval; they are routed to named views.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option For Against Postgres: full-text, pgvector, PostGIS Already in the stack; one query can combine text rank, vector distance, geography and tier; no new service Text relevance tuning and language analysis are basic; vector search slows at very large scale Amazon OpenSearch Service, managed domain Strong text relevance, language analysers, facets, hybrid text and vector scoring; proven at scale A cluster to size and pay for continuously; another store to keep in step OpenSearch Serverless No cluster sizing A capacity floor that is paid when idle; less control Bedrock Knowledge Bases, optionally with graph retrieval on Neptune Analytics Quick managed retrieval pipeline Chunking, tier filtering and citation behaviour are harder to control; our chunks must carry graph node ids and page-level provenance; ties retrieval to Bedrock Amazon S3 Vectors Very low-cost vector storage at large scale Vectors only; no text search; regional availability to confirm Amazon Kendra Managed enterprise search Cost; limited control over ranking and languages Self-hosted Qdrant, Weaviate or Elasticsearch Capable, open Another cluster for a small team

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Start with hybrid search inside Aurora PostgreSQL: full-text over original script and transliteration, vector search with pgvector, merged by reciprocal rank, filtered by geography and tier in the same query. Put retrieval behind one interface.

Move text and vector search to an OpenSearch Service domain when any of these is measured: relevance on the Marathi evaluation set stays below target after tuning; query latency exceeds target; the vector table outgrows comfortable Postgres sizes. Consider S3 Vectors as the store for older, rarely queried vectors.

Bedrock Knowledge Bases is not used for the main path. It is acceptable for a throwaway demo.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Marathi and Hindi tokenisation in Postgres is simple; transliteration and the glossary carry much of the load. This is the most likely reason to move.
  • Chunking follows document structure and every chunk stores document, page and node ids.

docs.title: To confirm
docs.text: Language analysis options in OpenSearch for Marathi; S3 Vectors availability in Mumbai.

docs.title: ADR 0008: A managed multilingual embedding model behind an interface, chosen by test
docs.text: Status: Proposed; the model is chosen after testing · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Vector search must work for Marathi, Hindi and English, including questions that mix them and names written in either script. Anthropic's platform is used here for generation, not embeddings, so the embedding model is a separate choice.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option For Against A multilingual embedding model on Amazon Bedrock (Amazon's Titan text embeddings or Cohere's multilingual model) No servers; pay per use; IAM Quality on Marathi is unknown until tested; availability in Mumbai to confirm; changing model means re-embedding An open multilingual model (for example BGE-M3 or multilingual E5) on a SageMaker endpoint or a Fargate task Full control; strong published multilingual results; no per-call fee An endpoint to run; a floor cost; we handle scaling An open model run only in batch jobs, with a small always-on task for queries Cheap for bulk embedding Two paths to maintain

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Define one embedding interface. Begin with a managed multilingual model on Bedrock for zero operations. Before the 30-day mark, compare it with one open model on a hundred real questions per language from the evaluation set, and keep whichever retrieves better for Marathi. Store the model name and version with every vector so a change is a clean re-embed from parsed text on S3.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Retrieval quality is reported by language; a model that helps English and hurts Marathi is rejected.
  • Re-embedding the corpus must be a scripted job.

docs.title: To confirm
docs.text: Which embedding models Bedrock offers in Mumbai and their documented language coverage.

docs.title: ADR 0009: Text layer first, Claude vision for scans, Tesseract to pre-screen
docs.text: Status: Accepted, pending a test on scanned Marathi papers · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Sources are PDFs: some with a text layer, some scanned, many in Marathi, many with tables (budget books, bills of quantity). The quote check needs page-level text.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option For Against PDF text layer (PyMuPDF) Free, exact, fast Only works when a text layer exists; table structure is lost Amazon Textract Managed; good at English forms and tables I could not confirm that it reads Devanagari; per-page cost Tesseract with Marathi and Hindi models Open, runs anywhere, handles Devanagari Weaker on poor scans and tables Claude reading page images Reads Devanagari and tables; can extract facts in the same pass Token cost per page; output must be checked Open layout models (for example docTR, PaddleOCR) on our own compute No per-page fee Operations; uneven Indic support

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Use the text layer when present.
  2. For scanned pages, send the page image to Claude for transcription and extraction together.
  3. Run Tesseract on scanned pages as a cheap independent reading. Where the quote from step 2 does not appear in either the text layer or the Tesseract output, mark the fact scan_unchecked so a person can review it.
  4. Use Textract only if a test shows it helps on English tables.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Scanned Marathi pages are the most expensive and least certain input. Their facts carry a visible mark until reviewed.
  • Budget tables are reconciled arithmetically against printed totals regardless of how they were read.

docs.title: To confirm
docs.text: Textract's language list; accuracy of each route on twenty scanned committee pages.

docs.title: ADR 0010: LangGraph on Fargate for workflows; EventBridge Scheduler for triggers
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Eight workflows order the work between agent sessions, code steps and human sign-offs. Runs may wait days for a reviewer. One workflow already exists as a LangGraph state graph.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option For Against LangGraph in a worker service, Postgres checkpointer Already written; pauses and resumes are first-class; fan-out per ward; plain Python next to the agent client; open source We host the worker; less visual tooling than a managed service AWS Step Functions Managed, durable, visual, strong retries; waits for callbacks cost nothing Workflow logic moves into a separate definition language; long agent sessions need callback plumbing; a second place for logic Airflow on MWAA, or Dagster Good for scheduled data pipelines Heavy and always-on; poor fit for human pauses and per-request flows Managed Agents scheduled deployments No scheduler to run Starts sessions only; cannot run code steps or gates; no one answers custom tool calls Temporal Durable execution, strong guarantees A cluster or a paid service; more than this needs

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
LangGraph runs in the worker service on Fargate with checkpoints in Aurora PostgreSQL. EventBridge Scheduler and S3 events put messages on SQS; the worker starts or resumes workflows from them. Agent sessions are started by the worker, not by Managed Agents deployments, so every run is launched, logged and authorised from our account and the worker is present to answer tool calls.

Step Functions is not used for workflow logic. It may be used later as a thin wrapper if an auditor wants a managed execution history.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The worker must survive restarts mid-run: workflows resume from the checkpoint, and nodes with side effects are written to be safe to repeat.
  • Human gates are rows in a review table; the review screen resumes the run.
  • The SQLite checkpointer in the starter code is replaced by the Postgres one in deployment.

docs.title: ADR 0011: Agents reach the graph through tools the worker answers; MCP only for the public data service
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Agents need read access to the graph. Managed Agents cloud sandboxes run outside our VPC. The graph database should have no public address.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option For Against Host an MCP server on a public address and attach it to agents Sessions run with no client attached; standard protocol A public, authenticated doorway into the query layer for our own agents; credentials in a vault; more attack surface Self-hosted sandboxes inside the VPC Tools run next to the data More to operate; cannot attach memory stores on Claude Platform on AWS Custom tools: the session asks, the worker answers from inside the VPC Graph and query layer stay private; tier and rate limits enforced in our code; nothing new exposed A worker must be attached for the life of each session; unattended scheduled deployments cannot be used Give agents a database snapshot as files No tools at all Stale; large; no tier filtering

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Agents get custom tools. The worker holds the session's event stream and answers each call by querying the api inside the VPC, with the tier of the user the session acts for. Intake agents get no graph tools at all; they receive an export of known entities as a file.

A separate, read-only MCP server is published for outside assistants and builders. It exposes only public-tier named views and is rate limited. Our own agents do not use it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Sessions are bound to a running worker, which fits ADR 0010.
  • Tool answers are logged with the session, the tier and the facts returned.
  • If unattended sessions are ever needed, the public MCP path can be extended with authentication instead of redesigning.

docs.title: ADR 0012: ECS Fargate and Lambda; no Kubernetes
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option For Against ECS on Fargate No servers or cluster to manage; per-task IAM roles; runs long-lived workers and streams; Spot for interruptible work Dearer per unit than instances; slower cold start than Lambda AWS Lambda Scales to zero; ideal for small event handlers Fifteen-minute limit; unsuited to holding agent event streams or long workflows Amazon EKS Portable; rich ecosystem A control plane and add-ons to run; more than a small team should carry EC2 instances Cheapest at steady load Patching and scaling by hand App Runner Simplest for a web service Less control over networking and background workers

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Four Fargate services: api, worker, loader, public-mcp. Lambda for small glue: S3 event handlers, WhatsApp webhook intake, scheduled checks. Bulk parsing and re-embedding run as Fargate tasks on Spot, started from a queue.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The worker holds long connections, so it is deployed with graceful draining and resumes from checkpoints.
  • Container images are the unit of release for everything except the static site.

docs.title: ADR 0013: SQS and EventBridge for events and schedules
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option For Against SQS queues with dead-letter queues; EventBridge Scheduler and rules Serverless, cheap, simple back-pressure and retries No replay of history beyond retention Amazon MSK or self-run Kafka Replayable log, high throughput A cluster for a workload of a few thousand events a day SNS only Simple fan-out No back-pressure

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: One queue per kind of work: new documents, scheduled runs, residents' messages, rebuild jobs. Each has a dead-letter queue with an alarm. EventBridge Scheduler creates the scheduled messages. Replay is not needed from the bus because the ledger on S3 is the replayable history (ADR 0001).

docs.title: ADR 0014: API behind CloudFront and a load balancer; Cognito for sign-in; tiers enforced in the query layer
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Concern Option For Against Entry CloudFront, WAF, Application Load Balancer to Fargate Streaming responses; one path for site and api; caching Fixed cost of a load balancer API Gateway to Fargate or Lambda Usage plans and keys built in Response-time and streaming limits; extra hop Identity Amazon Cognito Managed; phone and email sign-in; groups map to tiers Limited customisation Keycloak on Fargate Open, flexible Another service and database to run and secure Authorisation In the application only Simple Easy to miss a path Tier labels on data, filtered in the query layer An agent or endpoint cannot return what its tier may not see Every query path must go through the layer

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: CloudFront with WAF in front of an Application Load Balancer. Cognito user pools with groups for contributor, researcher, official and reviewer; anonymous use is the public tier. Every read goes through the query layer, which adds the caller's tier to the query. Public API keys and rate limits are handled in the api service.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• No service other than the loader and the query layer holds database credentials.
  • Researcher and official accounts are approved by a person.

docs.title: ADR 0015: Static site on S3 and CloudFront; MapLibre with PMTiles
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Concern Option For Against Hosting Static build on S3 behind CloudFront Cheapest, fastest, survives api outages with cached pages Build pipeline is ours Amplify Hosting Convenient previews Less control; another service Server-rendered app on Fargate Dynamic pages Cost and a new failure point Maps MapLibre with OpenStreetMap data as PMTiles on S3 Open; no per-request fee; Marathi labels possible; works offline for demos We build tiles Amazon Location Service Managed tiles, geocoding, routing Per-request cost; less control over local names

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: A static web application on S3 and CloudFront. Ward pages, briefs and scheme cards are pre-rendered at each release so they load without the api. Maps use MapLibre with PMTiles built from OpenStreetMap and stored on S3. Geocoding of local names uses our own glossary and road index first.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Most public traffic is served from the edge and costs little.
  • Phone-first design; pages must work on slow connections.

docs.title: ADR 0016: WhatsApp through AWS End User Messaging Social; Transcribe for voice notes
docs.text: Status: Accepted for WhatsApp text; speech pending tests · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Many residents will use WhatsApp, often by voice note in Marathi or Hindi.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Concern Option For Against WhatsApp AWS End User Messaging Social In the same account and IAM; an endpoint exists in Mumbai; events arrive on SNS Newer service; WhatsApp Business onboarding with Meta still applies Meta Cloud API direct No intermediary Webhook hosting and token handling are ours Twilio or another provider Mature tooling Extra vendor and cost Speech to text Amazon Transcribe, batch AWS lists Marathi and Hindi for batch jobs, and a voice note is a batch job Accuracy on local place names is unknown Open Indic models (AI4Bharat) on our compute, or the government's Bhashini service Built for Indian languages Operations, or dependence on an external service Text to speech Amazon Polly Hindi voices exist I found no Marathi voice Open Indic text-to-speech Marathi available Operations

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: WhatsApp through AWS End User Messaging Social. Voice notes are transcribed with Amazon Transcribe in batch mode; the transcript's place names are matched against the glossary and read back for confirmation before answering. Replies are text first. Spoken replies in Marathi are deferred until an open Indic model has been tested.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Messages are redacted before storage (ADR 0018).
  • WhatsApp's rules on message templates and reply windows shape how alerts are sent.

docs.title: To confirm
docs.text: Transcribe accuracy on fifty real Marathi voice notes; WhatsApp Business account approval for the host organisation.

docs.title: ADR 0017: Store everything in Mumbai (ap-south-1)
docs.text: Status: Accepted; one legal question open · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Users are in Mumbai. Most data is published civic documents. Some is residents' contributions, which are personal data under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. Model inference may run outside India.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: All stores and services run in ap-south-1. Residents' messages and images are redacted before storage and before any model call, so that what leaves the region for inference is the question and public facts, not identity. Contributors' account data never goes to a model.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Latency to users is low.
  • Some AWS features arrive later in Mumbai than elsewhere; each ADR lists what to confirm.
  • Model inference location is set by the Claude offering, not by this platform.

docs.title: To confirm
docs.text:
• With a lawyer: whether sending redacted residents' text for processing outside India needs notice or consent wording.
  • Which region serves Claude Platform on AWS requests and what inference geography options apply.

docs.title: ADR 0018: Security and privacy baseline
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Area Rule Network Databases and services in private subnets; only CloudFront and the load balancer are public; security groups allow service-to-store paths only Identity One IAM role per service with least privilege; no long-lived keys; SigV4 to Claude; people sign in through IAM Identity Center Secrets Secrets Manager; nothing secret in agent sandboxes, memory stores, prompts or logs Encryption KMS at rest for S3, Aurora and the graph; TLS everywhere Edge WAF managed rules, rate limits per address and per key Untrusted input Documents and messages are data; agents that read them cannot write, publish or reach the network; outputs are validated in code Personal data No private individuals stored; officials by post; faces, number plates, phone numbers and addresses removed at intake; contributors can delete their data Integrity Archive bucket versioned with object lock; ledger append-only; releases and corrections logged with approver Detection CloudTrail, GuardDuty and Security Hub in every account; alarms on unusual query volume and on dead-letter queues Supply chain Pinned dependencies and image scanning in CI; agent definitions changed only through reviewed pull requests

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Redaction runs before storage, so originals of residents' images are not kept.
  • A security review is part of the move from the lean to the standard profile.

docs.title: ADR 0019: CloudWatch and OpenTelemetry for operations; an evaluation gate for behaviour
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Concern Option For Against Metrics, logs, traces CloudWatch with the AWS OpenTelemetry distribution Managed, in-account, enough for four services Dashboards are plain Self-run Grafana, Prometheus, Loki Rich, open More to operate Model and agent traces Console session viewer, plus session and run records in our registry No setup; every thread and tool call visible Lives outside our dashboards Langfuse, self-hosted Open; prompt and cost analytics Another service and database OpenTelemetry export of API spans Standard; joins with service traces Beta on Claude Platform on AWS

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
CloudWatch for service metrics, logs and alarms, with OpenTelemetry traces from the services. For agents, record each session's id, agent versions, cost and outcome in the registry and link to the Console trace. Add Langfuse only if prompt-level analytics become a daily need.

Behaviour is guarded by the evaluation gate: every change to an agent, prompt, rule, ontology or retrieval setting runs the extraction, question and refusal sets in CI against staging, reported by route and by language, and needs an owner's approval to reach production.

Dashboards to build first: source freshness; quote-check pass rate; held-queue size; answers failing the citation check; cost per desk per day; evaluation trend.

docs.title: ADR 0020: Terraform or OpenTofu; three accounts
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option For Against Terraform or OpenTofu Widely known among volunteers; open; explicit plans to review State to manage; more verbose AWS CDK Real programming languages; high-level constructs Ties the infrastructure code to AWS and to one language CloudFormation directly Native Verbose; slower to write

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Infrastructure in Terraform, compatible with OpenTofu, with remote state in S3. Three accounts under one organisation for the standard profile: development, staging, production. The lean profile uses one account with two stages. Agent, environment and memory definitions are applied by the ant CLI from the same pipeline, with a dry-run plan on pull requests and apply on merge.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Anyone joining can read a plan before it runs.
  • The host organisation owns the accounts and the state bucket.

docs.title: ADR 0021: Two profiles, lean and standard
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Funding is uncertain. The service must be able to idle cheaply for months and still be correct, and to grow when a pilot succeeds. No prices are quoted here; price both profiles for Mumbai before choosing.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Maintain two profiles from the same code (design.md, section 8). Start lean. Move to standard when a public launch or a formal pilot requires availability across zones.

Cost rules for both:

Driver Control Extraction tokens Smallest capable model for reading; batch API for backlogs; each document read once per extractor version Audit and brief tokens Session budgets; schedules weekly, not daily, unless a source changed Answer tokens Routing serves most questions from named views with no agent; pages pre-rendered Always-on capacity Prefer services that scale down or pause; in the lean profile, one small graph instance Data transfer Static content and tiles from CloudFront; exports as files Fixed network cost In the lean profile, one NAT path and gateway endpoints for S3

Measure spend by desk and by workflow in the first month, then set budgets and alarms.

docs.title: Revisit when
docs.text: Idle cost of the lean profile exceeds what the host can sustain, or traffic makes pay-per-use dearer than fixed capacity.

docs.title: ADR 0022: Protect the archive and the ledger; rebuild everything else
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 15 November 2026

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Data Protection Document archive S3 versioning and object lock; replication to a second region in the standard profile Facts ledger S3 versioning; replication in the standard profile Accounts, subscriptions, reviews, workflow state Aurora automated backups and point-in-time recovery Graph, text index, vector index, metric tables Not backed up as primary protection; rebuilt from the ledger by a scripted job. Snapshots kept only to speed recovery. Ontology, rules, agents, prompts, rubrics, infrastructure Git

A full rebuild into an empty environment is rehearsed before launch and after any change of engine. Its duration is the recovery time for the projections and is recorded.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Losing the graph database is an inconvenience, not a loss of knowledge.
  • The data the platform cannot regenerate is small: accounts, review decisions and residents' contributions. That is where backup attention goes.
